factors/how-f-001-network-conditions.title: Network Conditions
factors/how-f-001-network-conditions.content:
Definition
The quality of a user’s network access, including bandwidth, latency, stability, and cost.
Why It Matters

Network availability directly affects product accessibility
Network conditions are constrained in low-income regions or mobile usage scenarios
Affects feature availability and user experience

Quantitative Criteria

Bandwidth: available data transfer rate (Kbps/Mbps)
Latency: round-trip time RTT (ms)
Stability: packet loss rate, frequency of connection drops
Cost: cost per unit of data (affects willingness to use)

Design Guidelines

Prioritize core functions with offline capability
Adaptive media quality (adjusted according to bandwidth)
Caching strategy to reduce repeated requests
Graceful degradation: provide basic functionality when the network is unavailable
Clearly communicate the current network state and expected wait times

Related Standards

None specific; use performance best practices


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (a large number of users worldwide still face network constraints)

factors/how-f-002-device-capability.title: Device Capability
factors/how-f-002-device-capability.content:
Definition
The hardware limitations of the user’s device in terms of computing power, storage space, sensors, battery, and so on.
Why It Matters

Users of older or low-end devices account for a considerable share
Battery life limits how long users can use the product and in which situations
Missing sensors affect feature availability (e.g., games requiring a gyroscope are unplayable without one)

Quantitative Criteria

Processing capability: CPU speed, core count, GPU performance
RAM: available memory size
Storage: remaining space
Sensors: whether GPS, camera, fingerprint, NFC, etc. are present
Battery: endurance, charging conditions

Design Guidelines

Detect device capability and dynamically scale down to lightweight functionality
Avoid requiring high-end hardware for a feature to run
Provide a “power-saving mode” option
Allow external devices as substitutes (e.g., an external keyboard)

Related Standards

Progressive Web Apps (PWA) capability detection


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (especially important in emerging markets)

factors/how-f-003-power-battery-life.title: Power & Battery Life
factors/how-f-003-power-battery-life.content:
Definition
The constraints that a device’s battery endurance, ease of charging, and power-management capabilities place on how users can use it.
Why It Matters

Insufficient endurance limits mobile usage scenarios and forces users to cut back usage or hunt for a charger
Difficult charging (proprietary connectors, few charging stations) affects usability
Some users cannot charge frequently (e.g., outdoor workers, older adults)

Quantitative Criteria

Battery life: battery endurance under typical usage (hours)
Charging time: time required to charge from 0 to 100%
Power threshold: power draw under different loads (W)
Power adapter: whether universal charging is supported (USB-C PD, wireless charging)

Design Guidelines

Provide a power-saving mode (reduce performance, disable non-essential features)
Optimize code and hardware power consumption (low-power algorithms, sleep strategies)
Let users view the battery level and an estimate of remaining use time
Support multiple charging methods (wired, wireless, external battery)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























Device TypeEndurance ConsiderationsSmartphonesModerate daily use, fast charging, wireless chargingLaptops8 hours of office work, USB-C charging, external batteryWearables7+ days on standby, magnetic charging, low-power sensorsMedical devicesExtended monitoring, backup battery, emergency charging
Related Standards

No mandatory standard; relies on energy-efficiency certification (e.g., Energy Star)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (critical for mobile devices)

factors/how-f-004-compatibility-requirem.title: Compatibility Requirements
factors/how-f-004-compatibility-requirem.content:
Definition
The ability of a system to work correctly across different platforms, browser versions, operating systems, and assistive technologies.
Why It Matters

User environments are highly fragmented
Enterprise environments often run older browsers or operating systems
Assistive technologies (screen readers, eye-tracking devices) need dedicated adaptation

Quantitative Criteria

Support matrix: the range of versions that must be supported (minimum and maximum)
Market coverage: the distribution of platforms used by the target user base
Assistive technology adaptation: whether the product passes mainstream AT testing (JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver)

Design Guidelines

Adopt a progressive enhancement strategy
Use standardized web APIs to avoid obsolete plug-ins
Test mainstream assistive technologies regularly
Provide polyfills or fallback implementations

Related Standards

WCAG conformance requirements
Platform-specific compatibility lists (e.g., Android fragmentation)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (essential for enterprise products)

factors/how-f-005-technical-environment.title: Technical Environment
factors/how-f-005-technical-environment.content:
Definition
The technical infrastructure and device conditions that a product or service depends on, including network connection quality, device performance, operating systems, the software ecosystem, peripheral compatibility, and the frequency of technology updates.
Why It Matters
Differences in technical environment directly affect the availability and performance of a product or service. For example, weak network conditions can make online features unavailable, older devices may not support new features, and missing peripherals can limit the available interaction methods. Taking the technical environment into account helps design products or services that remain at least usable under a wide range of technical conditions, or that offer a degraded experience, improving accessibility and fault tolerance.
Related Standards and References

WCAG 2.1: consideration of technology dependence (e.g., providing alternatives that do not depend on technology)
Backward-compatibility guidance in the HTML5 and ARIA specifications
National broadband penetration rates and network quality standards (e.g., ITU recommendations)
Device accessibility feature guides (e.g., Android accessibility services, iOS Accessibility)
Peripheral standards: USB, Bluetooth, HID (Human Interface Device) specifications

Suggested Quantification Methods

Network conditions: bandwidth (Mbps), latency (ms), packet loss rate, offline availability
Device performance: CPU performance, memory size, screen resolution, supported input methods
Software compatibility: supported operating system versions, browser support range, required plug-ins or frameworks
Peripheral support: support for alternative input devices (e.g., switches, eye trackers, voice control)
Upgrades and maintenance: automatic update capability, long-term support period (LTS)
Data sources: network speed test tools, device lab testing, market share data, user surveys

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Digital products: offline functionality, low-bandwidth mode, progressive web apps (PWA), support for older browsers, compatibility with screen readers and alternative input devices
Industrial design: whether the device works in the electromagnetic, dry factory environment, whether both wired and wireless modes are supported, how widely the tools needed for repair are available
Architecture design: Wi-Fi coverage inside the building, the network that elevator emergency communication systems depend on, interoperability of smart building systems
Interior design: network requirements of smart home devices, whether local control is supported without cloud dependence
Graphic design: software compatibility of print files, whether dedicated printers or post-processing equipment is required
Fashion design: charging methods for smart garments, the technologies data transfer depends on (e.g., NFC, BLE), whether it works with a companion mobile app

Common Pitfalls and Blind Spots

Assuming every user has a high-speed network and the latest devices
Designing only for features under ideal technical conditions and ignoring the degraded experience
Ignoring the interaction between technical literacy and the technical environment (e.g., older adults may own capable devices but still be unable to use advanced features)
Failing to account for regional differences in network infrastructure in global products
Over-reliance on a single platform or ecosystem (e.g., iOS-only or Windows-only support)

Suggested Design Keywords
Degraded experience, offline-first, backward compatibility, multi-platform support, standard interfaces, pluggability, low technical barrier, network adaptability, local-first

Factor card: Technical Environment
Version: 0.1

factors/how-f-006-assistive-tech-compati.title: Assistive Technology Compatibility
factors/how-f-006-assistive-tech-compati.content:
Definition
The interoperability between a product or service and assistive technology (AT), including screen readers, magnification software, speech recognition, eye trackers, switch devices, and Braille displays.
Why It Matters

AT is the bridge that lets people with disabilities use digital products; incompatibility means complete unusability
Regulations (e.g., WCAG, Section 508) mandate AT compatibility for some products
The AT ecosystem is fragmented, so mainstream combinations must be covered

Quantitative Criteria

Supported list: the list of AT combinations that passed testing (browser + OS + AT)
Feature coverage under AT: the proportion of product features that remain usable with AT
Test pass rate: the percentage of standard AT test cases passed
User testing: the success rate of real AT users completing tasks

Design Guidelines

Follow standard accessibility APIs (ARIA, AT-SPI, UIAutomation)
Ensure correct focus management and a sensible reading order
Provide text alternatives and keyboard operation support
Test mainstream AT: NVDA+Firefox, JAWS+Chrome, VoiceOver, TalkBack

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























Platform/DomainAT ExamplesWebscreen readers, voice control, keyboard navigationDesktop applicationsUI Automation, Linux OrcaMobileTalkBack (Android), VoiceOver (iOS)Hardware devicesswitch input, eye trackers, head-tracking devices
Related Standards

The success criteria of WCAG 2.x directly support AT
Section 508 (US), EN 301 549 (EU)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (core of accessibility conformance)

factors/how-f-007-input-output-capabilit.title: Input Output Capability
factors/how-f-007-input-output-capabilit.content:
Definition
The diversity, precision, and compatibility of the input methods a device supports (touch, keys, voice, gamepads, eye tracking) and the output methods it provides (screen, speaker, vibration, Braille).
Why It Matters

Users may lack a certain input capability (e.g., one-handed operation, visual impairment) or prefer another
Insufficient output channels exclude users with limited sensory perception
Environmental factors may restrict certain I/O (e.g., a noisy environment requires visual output)

Quantitative Criteria

Number of input channels: the variety of supported input methods (≥3 is preferable)
Precision requirements: touch target size, key travel, speech recognition accuracy
Number of output channels: supported output modalities (audio, visual, haptic)
Degree of customization: whether users can adjust I/O mappings (key remapping, vibration intensity)

Design Guidelines

Support multiple input and output channels
Allow users to remap or disable individual channels
Avoid depending on a single channel (e.g., touch-only or sound-only)
Provide standard APIs so custom input devices can be attached

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainI/O ExamplesMobile appstouch, voice, Bluetooth keyboard, vibration, screen readingGaming devicesgamepads, motion sensing, VR controllers, steering wheelsIndustrial controlphysical buttons, knobs, foot pedals, indicator lights, buzzersWearablesbuttons, touchpads, voice, vibration, small display
Related Standards

Platform accessibility guides (iOS VoiceOver, Android TalkBack)
Gaming accessibility standards (Xbox Adaptive Controller)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (hardware-dependent products)

factors/how-f-008-authentication-burden.title: Authentication & Identity Burden
factors/how-f-008-authentication-burden.content:
Definition
The multidimensional cognitive, sensory, motor, and time burden that users face when completing identity authentication, account management, credential storage, and recovery. The core dimensions include:

Diversity of authentication methods: passwords, biometrics (fingerprint/face/voiceprint), hardware keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn), magic links, OTP, single sign-on (SSO), third-party federated login
Burden types:

Cognitive burden: recalling complex passwords, understanding security questions, recognizing phishing
Sensory burden: CAPTCHA recognition (visual/auditory), face recognition requires adequate lighting, fingerprint scanning requires clean fingertips
Motor burden: typing long passwords, operating hardware keys, completing gesture verification
Time burden: waiting for SMS/email, multi-factor authentication flows, account recovery flows


Credential management burden: password manager compatibility, cross-device synchronization, backup and recovery, legacy inheritance
Exclusivity risk: a single authentication method (face only/password only/SMS only) absolutely excludes users with particular capabilities

How this differs from other factors:

WHO-F-001/003/009/010: user capability states
WHAT-F-002/003: task cognitive load / fault tolerance
This factor focuses on the multi-channel burden and exclusivity risk of authentication as a specific technical task

Why It Matters

Password fatigue: the average user manages 100+ accounts, and complexity requirements lead to reuse or passwords written on paper
Biometric exclusion: worn or missing fingerprints; face recognition fails for dark-skinned users, users wearing head coverings, and users wearing glasses; voiceprints fail for people who have undergone laryngeal surgery
Hardware key barrier: they must be purchased, carried, plugged in, and protected from loss
SMS/email OTP: depends on network/phone number, adds latency, and carries SIM-swapping risk
Account recovery: security-question answers are vulnerable to social engineering, backup email accounts are lost, manual review cycles are long
WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 mandate: at least one authentication path that does not rely on a test of cognitive function

Design Response (Alternative)
Provide at least two independent authentication paths with differing capability requirements, and let users choose:





































































Authentication PathCognitiveVisualAuditoryMotorSuitable ForPassword + password manager autofillLowLowLowMediumMost usersBiometrics (fingerprint/face)NoneMediumNoneLowUsers with motor or cognitive limitationsFIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keyLowLowLowMediumHigh-security needs / enterprise usersMagic link / email OTPLowMediumNoneLowInfrequent sign-ins / users without a deviceSMS / voice OTPLowNoneMediumLowUsers without a smartphone / users with visual impairmentsSingle sign-on (SSO / federated login)LowLowLowLowEnterprise / multi-system usersTrusted device / session extensionNoneNoneNoneNoneFrequent users / high cognitive load
Key principles:

Never force a single authentication method (WCAG SC 3.3.8 Level A)
Users can switch between authentication methods seamlessly, without re-enrolling
Account recovery must not depend on cognitive tests (such as security questions); use trusted contacts, trusted devices, or hardware keys instead
Password manager autofill must work flawlessly (no autocomplete=off blocking)

Cross-Domain Mapping






























DomainExclusion ExampleInclusion ExampleDigital productsPassword-only sign-in, CAPTCHA without an audio option, password managers blockedOptional multi-factor, WebAuthn, magic links, session extensionIndustrial designDevice pairing requires a complex PIN, control only through a phone appNFC-tag pairing, physical-button confirmation, web control panelArchitecture designAccess control limited to face/fingerprint, visitors must register manually at the front deskMultimodal access control (card/code/biometric/remote unlock), temporary visitor access codesFashion designSmart garments pair only through an app and require re-authentication after washingPhysical-button pairing, NFC tags, basic functions that require no authentication
Measurement Dimensions

Number of authentication methods (≥2 independent paths, WCAG conformance)
Capability requirements labeled per path (cognitive/visual/auditory/motor)
Password manager autofill compatibility (pass/fail)
Account recovery success rate and average elapsed time
Task abandonment rate caused by authentication failure

Related Standards and References

WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8: Accessible Authentication (Minimum) — Level A mandate
EN 301 549 9.3.3.8 — EU procurement standard with the same clause lineage
NIST SP 800-63B — authenticator assurance levels (AAL1/2/3)
FIDO2 / WebAuthn — passwordless authentication standard
ISO/IEC 29115 entity authentication assurance framework

B1 Cross-Reference Note
This factor was added by the INCL-XREF-001 GAP-3 determination: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 provides ready-made Level A evidence and maps directly; the other four benchmarks have no structured factor for “authentication burden.”

factors/rul-001-accessibility-compliance.title: Accessibility Regulation Compliance
factors/rul-001-accessibility-compliance.content:
Definition
The accessibility provisions within the laws and regulations that products and spaces must comply with.
Why It Matters

Violations can lead to lawsuits, fines, and product withdrawal
They are entry barriers for certain markets
They concern social responsibility and brand value

Quantitative Criteria

Specific standards: WCAG 2.1 AA, Section 508, EN 301 549, etc.
Coverage: the proportion of success criteria satisfied
Self-assessment / third-party audit: pass rate

Design Guidelines

Treat regulatory requirements as the minimum bar
Keep records of compliance checks
Resolve critical compliance items first
Watch for regulatory updates and iterate accordingly

Related Standards

WCAG 2.1/2.2 (the global web standard)
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA, US)
EN 301 549 (EU ICT products)
GB/T 37668-2019 (China’s internet content accessibility)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (mandatory, high risk)

factors/rul-002-data-privacy-compliance.title: Data Privacy Compliance
factors/rul-002-data-privacy-compliance.content:
Definition
Compliance with privacy-related regulations across the entire data lifecycle: collection, storage, processing, and sharing.
Why It Matters

Severe penalties (up to 4% of global turnover under GDPR)
Central to user trust
Cross-border business must satisfy the requirements of different jurisdictions

Quantitative Criteria

Consent rate: the proportion of users who give valid consent
Data minimization: whether the types of data collected exceed what is necessary
Retention period: whether storage limits are defined and deletion is enforced
User rights response: turnaround time for deletion, correction, and portability requests

Design Guidelines

Privacy by Design principles
Clear privacy policy and usage instructions
Provide a permissions management interface so users can withdraw consent at any time
Capability to anonymize data

Related Standards

GDPR (EU)
CCPA/CPRA (California)
PIPL (China’s Personal Information Protection Law)
ISO/IEC 27701 (privacy information management)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (legally mandated)

factors/rul-003-safety-certification.title: Safety Certification Requirements
factors/rul-003-safety-certification.content:
Definition
The safety standards and certification systems that a product or service must pass — such as CE safety conformity, UL certification, FDA/CE MDR for medical devices, ISO 26262 for automotive, and DO-178C for aviation — ensuring that it causes no harm to users.
Why It Matters

Uncertified products cannot be sold or used in certain markets
Safety incidents can trigger recalls, lawsuits, and criminal liability
Safety certification raises user trust and may earn insurance premiums

Quantitative Criteria

Certification coverage: the number of safety standards met by each product module
Test pass rate: the proportion of safety test cases passed (must approach 100%)
Residual risk level: the severity and probability of unresolved risks
Certification status: whether a valid certificate is held and the re-evaluation cycle

Design Guidelines

Consider target certifications from the requirements stage, folding safety requirements in from the start
Work with certification bodies to run pre-compliance testing
Design traceable safety documentation (hazard analysis, risk assessment)
Build in safety margins (redundancy, fault protection)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainCertification ExamplesMedical devicesFDA 510(k), CE MDR, ISO 13485Automotive electronicsISO 26262 (functional safety), UNECE R155 (cybersecurity)Industrial machineryCE Machinery Directive, UL certificationConsumer electronicsCE safety, battery safety (UN38.3), RoHS
Related Standards

ISO 31000: risk management
IEC 62304: medical device software lifecycle
Mandatory safety standards for each industry


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (heavily regulated domains)

factors/rul-004-ip-compliance.title: Intellectual Property Compliance
factors/rul-004-ip-compliance.content:
Definition
All content used by a product (images, fonts, audio, video) and all technology it uses (algorithms, libraries, code, patents) must be lawfully licensed or covered by a permissive license agreement, so as not to infringe others’ copyrights, trademarks, or patents.
Why It Matters

Infringement lawsuits can lead to product withdrawal, heavy damages, and reputational damage
Open-source licenses (GPL, MIT, Apache) carry copyleft-style provisions that constrain how the overall release must be distributed
Enterprise procurement places strict requirements on IP cleanliness

Quantitative Criteria

License inventory: all licenses of project dependencies and their restrictions
Compliance rate: the proportion of assets with a clear license or grant
Patent risk: whether the technologies used fall within third-party patent claims
Third-party content: whether assets come from licensed libraries or have been purchased

Design Guidelines

Prefer open-source or public-domain resources, and comply with their licenses
Establish a content review process to ensure every asset has a lawful source
Record IP provenance and proof of authorization
Seek legal advice or replace assets when IP status is uncertain

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainIP ConsiderationsSoftware developmentthird-party library licenses, code reuse, patent poolsDigital contentimage/font/music copyrights, derivative-work permissionsHardware productschip IP cores, standard-essential patents (SEPs) in communicationsBrand designtrademark use, references to competitor elements, the limits of parody
Related Standards

Copyright, patent, and trademark law in each jurisdiction
Open-source licenses (GPL, MIT, BSD, Apache)
Patent policies of standards organizations (IEEE, 3GPP)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (compliance and legal risk control)

factors/rul-005-ethics-review.title: Ethics Review
factors/rul-005-ethics-review.content:
Definition
The ethical principles and review mechanisms that a product or service must pass or follow — including user autonomy, informed consent, dignity of data, fairness, non-maleficence, and explainability — especially where user research, data collection, and algorithmic decision-making are involved.
Why It Matters

Ethical violations lead to loss of credibility, user backlash, and regulatory intervention
Bias in AI systems, dark patterns, and manipulative design spark ethical controversy
Research projects must pass institutional ethics committee (IRB) review

Quantitative Criteria

Ethics checklist completeness: whether all ethical topics are covered
Informed consent rate: the proportion of users who consent to study terms (and their level of understanding)
Algorithmic fairness metrics: prediction disparities across demographic groups
Complaints and disputes: the number of ethics-related user complaints

Design Guidelines

Introduce ethical assessment early (design ethics workshops)
Provide a clear, understandable informed consent process (not lengthy terms)
Avoid dark patterns (click inducement, hiding cancellation)
Ensure algorithmic explainability and a channel of appeal
Establish an ethics feedback channel

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainEthics PrioritiesUser researchinformed consent, privacy protection, participant rightsAI systemsfairness, transparency, accountability, non-discriminationSocial platformsethics of using user data, fairness of content moderationGame designaddiction prevention, gambling mechanics, addictive design
Related Standards

Belmont Report: ethical principles (respect, beneficence, justice)
GDPR: data protection and consent
IEEE Ethically Aligned Design
Institutional IRB guidelines


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (key for social impact and trust)

factors/rul-006-industry-standards.title: Industry Specific Standards
factors/rul-006-industry-standards.content:
Definition
Safety and quality norms specific to particular industries (healthcare, finance, education, aviation, etc.).
Why It Matters

Industry entry barriers
Professional certification requirements
Safety and quality standards

Quantification Criteria

Certification level: whether a specific certification is met (e.g., HIPAA, FISMA)
Audit pass rate: proportion of internal audit requirements satisfied
Security vulnerability severity: number of high-severity vulnerabilities

Design Guidelines

Understand the specialized requirements of the target industry
Build compliance needs in from the earliest design stages
Documentation and audit-trail capability

Related Standards

Healthcare: HIPAA, GDPR health data
Finance: PCI DSS, GLBA, SOX
Education: FERPA (student privacy)
Aviation: DO-178C (avionics software)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (varies by industry)

factors/rul-007-policies-regulations.title: Policies & Regulations
factors/rul-007-policies-regulations.content:
Definition
Legal, regulatory, standards, and policy requirements affecting the design, production, distribution, and use of a product or service, including accessibility legislation, data privacy regulations, product safety standards, environmental requirements, and government procurement policies.
Why It Matters
Policies and regulations are external constraints that design must comply with. Ignoring compliance can leave a product unable to reach the market, expose it to legal action, or exclude it from government procurement. Considering policies and regulations helps mitigate risks early, capture policy benefits (such as tax incentives and subsidies), and ensure the product’s legality and sustainability in its target markets.
Related Standards and References

Accessibility legislation by country: e.g., the US ADA, the EU accessibility directive, China’s Law on the Construction of a Barrier-Free Environment
Data privacy regulations: e.g., GDPR, CCPA, PIPL
Product safety standards: e.g., CE marking, UL certification, FCC compliance
Environmental regulations: e.g., RoHS, REACH, Energy Star
Government procurement policies: e.g., US Section 508, EU EN 301 549
Industry self-regulatory standards: e.g., W3C WCAG, ISO accessibility standards

Suggested Quantification Methods

Compliance checklist: satisfaction of mandatory requirements derived from applicable laws and regulations (yes/no)
Certification status: whether required certifications have been obtained (e.g., accessibility certification, safety certification)
Degree of policy leverage: whether tax relief, subsidies, or government procurement preferences are being captured
Regulatory update tracking: timeliness of monitoring regulatory changes
Data sources: legal and regulatory texts, certification bodies, government procurement portals, legal counsel

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: web accessibility legal compliance, data privacy protection (e.g., GDPR), children’s online privacy protection (COPPA)
Industrial design: product safety standards, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), energy efficiency labels, material restrictions (e.g., RoHS)
Architecture: building accessibility codes, fire safety standards, energy efficiency standards
Interior design: furniture safety standards, fire-retardant material requirements, indoor air quality standards
Graphic design: advertising content regulations, mandatory label information, restricted substances (e.g., heavy metals in inks)
Fashion design: textile safety standards, flammability regulations, banned dye restrictions, product labeling regulations

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Treating compliance as equivalent to best practice, overlooking that regulations are often minimum standards
Focusing only on domestic regulations while ignoring the requirements of target export markets
Treating compliance as a late-stage check rather than an early design consideration
Overlooking industry self-regulatory standards or customer-specific requirements (e.g., additional clauses in enterprise procurement)
Lagging regulatory updates leaving designs outdated

Design Recommendation Keywords
Compliance checking, regulatory foresight, certification readiness, policy leverage, standards tracking, legal counsel, risk assessment, market entry requirements

factors/what-f-001-task-complexity.title: Task Complexity
factors/what-f-001-task-complexity.content:
Definition
A composite measure of the number of steps a task requires, the number of decision points, the amount of information, and the skill demands involved.
Why It Matters
Complexity directly affects:

Learning cost
Error probability
Task abandonment rate
User satisfaction

Quantification Criteria

Step count: the minimum number of operations needed to complete a task
Decision points: the number of nodes where the user must make a decision
Information volume: the number of information elements presented simultaneously

Design Guidelines

Divide and conquer: break complex tasks into multiple simple subtasks
Provide task templates and wizards
Use default values and smart recommendations to reduce the decision burden
Progressive disclosure: reveal advanced options step by step

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Digital products: step-by-step wizards, default configurations, smart recommendations
Industrial design: modular design, one-touch operation
Architecture: clear spatial zoning, well-defined functional circulation
Fashion design: simplified dressing steps, multifunctional design

Related Standards

Miller’s Law: the 7±2 information-chunking principle
Hick’s Law: the more choices there are, the longer the decision takes


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (core factor)

factors/what-f-002-cognitive-load.title: Cognitive Load
factors/what-f-002-cognitive-load.content:
Definition
The total amount of mental effort a user must invest while carrying out a task.
Why It Matters
Excessive cognitive load leads to:

Longer task completion times
Higher error rates
More user frustration and abandonment

Quantification Criteria

Measurement methods: NASA-TLX scale, pupil diameter, task completion time
Threshold: task cognitive load is generally expected to stay at or below a moderate level (NASA-TLX score < 60)
Influencing factors: information density, time pressure, task complexity, technical literacy

Design Guidelines

Reduce working memory burden (step-by-step guidance, progressive presentation)
Provide default values and smart recommendations
Use clear information layering and visual hierarchy
Provide undo/redo mechanisms to lower the decision burden

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Digital products: fewer pop-ups, simplified flows, immediate help
Industrial design: simplified control panels, fewer operating steps, clear labeling
Architecture: clear wayfinding systems, simplified navigation paths
Fashion design: ease of putting on, simplified donning and doffing steps

Related Standards

ISO 9241-210: usability engineering standard
WCAG 3.0: cognitive accessibility guidelines


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (extremely broad impact)

factors/what-f-003-fault-tolerance.title: Fault Tolerance Requirement
factors/what-f-003-fault-tolerance.content:
Definition
The degree to which a system tolerates user errors and abnormal situations, and its ability to recover from them.
Why It Matters

Lowers user anxiety (users know that mistakes will not lead to catastrophic consequences)
Encourages exploration and learning
Reduces training costs

Quantification Criteria

Undo depth: how many steps of undo are supported
Confirmation mechanisms: whether critical operations require confirmation
Error prevention: mechanisms that prevent errors (e.g., disabling dangerous buttons)
Recovery time: time needed to return from an error to a normal state

Design Guidelines

Provide clear, useful error messages
Make actions easy to undo (undo button, Ctrl+Z, history)
Require secondary confirmation for high-risk operations
Autosave and version snapshots
Clear recovery paths

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Digital products: undo/redo, confirmation dialogs, autosave
Physical devices: emergency stop buttons, safety switches
Architectural spaces: redundant exits, safety-net design
Fashion design: easy on/off design, adjustable parts

Related Standards

ISO 9241-110: error tolerance principle


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (safety-related)

factors/what-f-004-task-persistence.title: Task Persistence Requirement
factors/what-f-004-task-persistence.content:
Definition
Whether a task requires continuity over long spans (across sessions or devices), and how strongly data saving and state restoration are needed.
Why It Matters

Users may lose progress to interruptions, leading to frustration and abandonment
Some tasks inherently take a long time to complete (e.g., filling out long forms, creating content)
Persistence design improves user completion rates and satisfaction

Quantification Criteria

Average task completion time: expected duration (minutes/hours/days)
Interruption frequency: average number of times a user is interrupted per hour
Resumption cost: time and cognitive burden needed to restart the task
Storage requirements: amount and types of data that must be saved (drafts, settings, history)

Private and Sensitive Task Scenarios

Reinforced by the B1 cross-reference pass (INCL-XREF-001, cross-referenced against WHO ICF d5-d6 self-care and domestic life)

Task persistence carries special requirements in private tasks:

Toilet/changing/showering tasks: waterproofing, slip resistance, easy cleaning, privacy protection, quick completion
Medical/medication/monitoring tasks: privacy, accuracy, reminders, data recording, must not be lost
Financial/legal/identity-verification tasks: security, shoulder-surfing protection, audit trails, revocability
Menstrual/incontinence/stoma-care tasks: discretion, easy access, leak prevention, no embarrassment, quick completion
Mental health/counseling tasks: anonymity, safe exit, local data encryption, no trace left behind

Design implication: the “persistence” of private tasks is not just technical saving; it also spans safety dimensions such as privacy boundaries, revocability, and trace-free exit.
Design Guidelines

Autosave (input, progress, personalization settings)
Support multi-device sync (cloud sync, local sync)
Provide a “continue where you left off” entry point
Version history and rollback capability
Resumable transfers (large-file upload/download)
Private-task specific: anonymous mode, locally encrypted storage, one-tap trace clearing, panic exit key

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Related Standards

No unified standard; best practice depends on the scenario
Pending WP-C linkage: ISO 27001 information security (data protection for private tasks)

factors/what-f-005-task-collaboration.title: Task Collaboration
factors/what-f-005-task-collaboration.content:
Definition
Whether a task requires multiple users/roles to complete it together, and the synchronization, division-of-labor complexity, and information-sharing needs of that collaboration.
Why It Matters

Collaborative tasks place special demands on communication, coordination, and role division
Power imbalances, difficulty synchronizing schedules, and information asymmetry may exist
Design must foster effective collaboration and reduce its cost

Quantification Criteria

Number of participants: required headcount range (2+, 2-5, 5+)
Synchronization requirement: must be real-time vs. can be asynchronous
Division-of-labor flexibility: how flexibly the task can be decomposed (fixed roles vs. flexible sharing)
Dependency strength: how tightly the task steps depend on one another

Design Guidelines

Clarify roles and permissions to avoid confusion over responsibilities
Provide shared views with real-time updates (e.g., co-editing)
Support asynchronous collaboration (comments, task assignment, status tracking)
Reduce unnecessary communication overhead (automated notifications, progress digests)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainCollaboration FeaturesOnline documentsMulti-user simultaneous editing, comments, @mentions, version historyProject managementTask assignment, progress boards, reminders, document sharingSocial appsGroup chats, collaborative posts, co-creationHome spacesShared shopping lists, shared calendars, chore reminders
Related Standards

Cooperative system design principles (e.g., CSCW, groupware)
ISO 9241-410: support for collaborative work in interactive systems


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (core for team collaboration tools)

factors/what-f-006-task-interruption-tol.title: Task Interruption Tolerance
factors/what-f-006-task-interruption-tol.content:
Definition
Whether a task may be paused or interrupted, and how easily it must be resumed afterward. Related to persistence but focused on the user experience “when the interruption happens”.
Why It Matters

In real environments users are often interrupted by calls, notifications, and other people
Tasks with low interruption tolerance need interruption-proof design
Interruptions easily lose state or cause errors (e.g., accidental touches)

Quantification Criteria

Interruption recovery time: average time for a user to return to the task state after an interruption
Interruption cost: degree of data loss or progress rollback caused by the interruption
Do-not-disturb needs: how often and how strongly users use do-not-disturb modes
Asynchronous support: whether the task supports a “start now, finish later” mode (e.g., booking, queueing)

Design Guidelines

Clearly mark “unsaved changes” together with recovery options
Provide a “handle it later” mechanism (save as a to-do, reminder notifications)
Let users actively enable a “focus mode” (blocking non-urgent notifications)
Interruption-point design: chunk the task so that each chunk is relatively self-contained

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainInterruption HandlingForms/surveysSave drafts, allow filling out over multiple sittingsMeetings/livestreamsRecording playback, notes synced to timestampsTransaction flowsPersistent shopping carts, staged ordersCreation toolsMulti-step undo, snapshots, branched history
Related Standards

Common UX patterns: autosave, drafts, offline queues


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (important for focus-intensive task products)

factors/when-f-001-usage-time-period.title: Usage Time Period
factors/when-f-001-usage-time-period.content:
Definition
Users’ subjective preference for the time periods in which they use a product (e.g., morning, late night, working hours, weekends), which may not match the time actually available to them.
Why It Matters

Use during preferred time periods brings higher satisfaction and efficiency
Period preferences affect UI themes (dark mode at night) and notification timing
Understanding preferences supports personalized recommendations and user segmentation

Quantification Criteria

Period distribution data: heatmaps of user active times
Self-reported preference: survey questions such as “When do you prefer to use it?”
Period switching frequency: whether users stick to fixed usage periods
Period satisfaction: experience ratings for different time periods

Design Guidelines

Let users set “usual usage periods” to optimize reminders and notifications
Adjust the interface automatically (dark at night, bright in the morning)
Offer different content or feature recommendations for different periods
Respect do-not-disturb settings; avoid interrupting users outside their preferred periods

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainTime-of-Day AdaptationContent platformsPersonalized push timing, period-exclusive contentFitness appsRecommended workout times, morning wake-up, sleep-aid meditationSocial appsNight mode, good-morning greetings, bedtime remindersSmart homesLighting and temperature adjusted automatically to user habits
Related Standards

No mandatory standard; behavioral analytics and user research methods


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (important for content consumption products)

factors/when-f-002-usage-frequency.title: Usage Frequency
factors/when-f-002-usage-frequency.content:
Definition
How frequently users use the product, covering different frequency patterns such as daily, weekly, and occasional.
Why It Matters

The needs of high-frequency and low-frequency users differ greatly (feature depth vs. quick onboarding)
Frequency affects the learning curve, memory retention, and feature-discovery strategies
Low-frequency users may need more memory aids and revisit incentives

Quantification Criteria

DAU/MAU ratio: ratio of daily average actives to monthly actives (a stickiness measure)
Session interval: average time between two uses
Frequency distribution: share of high/medium/low-frequency users
Duration per session: average duration of a single use

Design Guidelines

High-frequency users: provide shortcuts, batch operations, and entry points to advanced features
Low-frequency users: simplify the interface, give clear guidance, and show recent-usage history
Let users set a preferred frequency or auto-adjust difficulty
Design revisit mechanisms aimed at next-month retention (email, notifications)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainFrequency AdaptationTool softwarePin frequently used features, history records, saved templatesSocial appsAdjustable push frequency, aggregated important events, daily digestsFitness appsPeriodized training plans, rest reminders, achievement systemsPublic servicesBooking systems, saved frequently used information, express lanes
Related Standards

None specific; engagement metrics are common in analytics


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (critical for retention and engagement)

factors/when-f-003-seasonality.title: Seasonality
factors/when-f-003-seasonality.content:
Definition
The influence of seasonal climate change (temperature, humidity, daylight duration, holiday distribution, etc.) on the use of a product/service.
Why It Matters

User needs and environmental conditions differ greatly across seasons (e.g., sun protection in summer, warmth in winter)
Holiday patterns change users’ time availability and social settings
Ignoring seasonality can leave features idle or make the experience uncomfortable

Quantification Criteria

Climate parameters: temperature range, rainfall, hours of sunshine
Seasonal usage rates: fluctuation in daily actives/visits across seasons
Holiday effects: usage peaks before and during holidays
Seasonal constraints: number of days of extreme weather (heat waves, severe cold, rainy season)

Design Guidelines

Offer seasonal themes or interfaces (e.g., darker in winter, brighter in summer)
Seasonal feature toggles (e.g., rainy-season reminders, insect protection)
Adjust operational strategies (seasonal merchandise, seasonal content pushes)
Consider climate effects on hardware (waterproofing, temperature tolerance)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainAdaptation ExamplesOutdoor productsUV index alerts, rain-gear carry reminders, anti-slip designDigital servicesHoliday theme skins, seasonal event pushes, seasonal content recommendationsFashion designSeasonal fabrics, detachable layers, breathability/warmth balanceArchitectureShading, insulation, ventilation, rainwater harvesting
Related Standards

No mandatory standard; refer to meteorological data and seasonal marketing best practices


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (important for users in outdoor/seasonal scenarios)

factors/when-f-004-time-pressure.title: Time Pressure
factors/when-f-004-time-pressure.content:
Definition
The urgency users feel under external time limits, and how well the time needed to complete a task matches the time they expected.
Why It Matters
Time pressure causes:

Increased cognitive load
Reduced decision quality
User anxiety and frustration
Higher error rates

Quantification Criteria

Time limits: whether the task has a hard deadline
Response time requirements: the response time window users expect (e.g., within 2 seconds)
Tolerance: users’ time tolerance thresholds for different tasks

Design Guidelines

Show remaining time or progress indicators
Allow pausing/extending time (e.g., an extendable exam countdown)
Provide express paths (alternative flows with fewer steps)
Avoid unnecessary waiting and loading

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Digital products: loading animations, progress bars, allowing draft saving
Industrial design: fast startup, one-touch completion of common tasks
Architecture: clearly marked emergency evacuation routes
Service design: express lane options, appointment time selection

Related Standards

Nielsen Norman Group: response time thresholds (0.1 s perceived as instant, 1 s keeps the flow, 10 s holds attention)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (high impact on real-time interaction)

factors/when-f-005-time-availability.title: Time Availability
factors/when-f-005-time-availability.content:
Definition
The total time and time windows users can allocate to using a product in a day or a week (e.g., only during commuting, lunch breaks, or evenings).
Why It Matters

Users’ available time directly caps task length and feature complexity
Fragmented time requires task chunking and quick resumption
Differences in time availability affect feature prioritization and onboarding strategies

Quantification Criteria

Available minutes per day: self-reported by users or inferred from usage data
Degree of time fragmentation: number and length of available time blocks (e.g., 3×15 min vs 1×2 h)
Regularity: whether the user is available at fixed times every day
Time-conflict frequency: how often planned tasks are interrupted by other matters

Design Guidelines

Support task chunking with resumable breakpoints
Provide “continue later” and scheduled reminders
Let users set a daily target duration
For long tasks, provide estimated completion times and step-by-step plans

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainTime AdaptationLearning platformsMicro-courses, lesson segmentation, study plansReading appsChapter paging, reading progress, bookmarksOnline formsAuto drafts, step-by-step saving, resume entry pointProject managementTask breakdown, time estimates, progress reminders
Related Standards

No standard; based on user research and behavioral analytics


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (important for fragmented-time use cases)

factors/when-f-006-fatigue-level.title: Fatigue Level
factors/when-f-006-fatigue-level.content:
Definition
The degree to which a user’s cognitive and physiological abilities decline after continuous use or during specific time periods, manifesting as distractibility, rising error rates, and slower operation.
Why It Matters

Operating under fatigue increases risk (e.g., in medical and driving scenarios)
Fatigue leads to user abandonment and degraded experience
Detecting and responding to fatigue improves safety and sustained use

Quantification Criteria

Session length vs error rate: the error growth curve over time in use
Pupillometry / blink rate: physiological fatigue signals (when sensors are available)
Self-reported fatigue: the level of fatigue the user reports periodically
Reaction time: increasing delay in operational responses

Design Guidelines

Detect and act on fatigue signals (e.g., consecutive errors, slower operation)
Prompt rest proactively (micro-breaks, eye exercises)
Simplify the interface under fatigue (reduce information, enlarge key elements)
Support pausing and checkpoint saving

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainFatigue responseDriving systemsFatigue monitoring, rest reminders, lane-keeping assistanceOffice softwareScheduled break reminders, eye-care mode, document summarizationIndustrial controlRest scheduling between work periods, fatigue early-warning systemsLearning platformsLearning-pace regulation, attention detection, chunked content
Related Standards

ISO 9241-410: fatigue considerations in human factors engineering
Industry safety regulations (e.g., aviation, healthcare)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Key for safety- and health-related design)

factors/where-f-001-physical-environment.title: Physical Environment
factors/where-f-001-physical-environment.content:
Definition
The characteristics of the physical space in which a product or service is used, including natural or man-made physical conditions such as lighting, noise, temperature, spatial layout, accessibility, terrain, and climate.
Why It Matters
The physical environment directly affects whether users can effectively perceive, operate, and use a product or service. For example, strong light can cause screen glare, noise can interfere with voice interaction, and spatial constraints can block wheelchair access. Considering the physical environment helps design solutions suited to a variety of usage situations, improving reliability and comfort.
Related Standards and References

ISO 21542: accessibility of the built environment (corridor width, slopes, lighting, etc.)
ANSI/ASA S12.60: classroom acoustics standard
OSHA noise exposure limits
IEQ (indoor environmental quality) standards: e.g., ASHRAE 62.1 (ventilation), IESNA lighting standards
Environmental factors in ergonomics: e.g., the effects of temperature and humidity on comfort and performance

Suggested Quantification Methods

Lighting: illuminance (lux), uniformity, glare index (UGR), color temperature (kelvin)
Noise: equivalent continuous sound level (Leq, dBA), Speech Transmission Index (STI)
Temperature and humidity: dry-bulb temperature, relative humidity, WBGT (wet-bulb globe temperature)
Spatial accessibility: door width, corridor width, turning radius, slope ratio
Climate protection: IP rating (dust/water resistance), operating temperature range
Data sources: environmental measurement instruments, standard test procedures, user context studies

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: anti-glare screens, adjustable brightness, noise-cancelling microphones, dust/water resistance ratings (IP68), readability in bright light
Industrial design: protection ratings, operating temperature ranges, vibration tolerance, easy-to-clean surfaces
Architectural design: slopes, handrails, door widths, stair treads, and non-slip flooring compliant with accessible design
Interior design: furniture tip-over prevention, curtain blackout performance, sound-absorbing materials, damp-proofing treatment
Graphic design: wind- and water-resistant outdoor advertising, detachable structures, weather-resistant inks
Fashion design: waterproof breathable fabrics, thermal insulation, sun protection factor (UPF), quick-drying performance

Common Pitfalls and Blind Spots

Considering only ideal laboratory conditions and ignoring the changing conditions of real use
Assuming all users operate the product in the same physical environment
Focusing only on extreme conditions (e.g., underwater, high heat) and ignoring everyday mild adverse factors (e.g., a slightly bright room)
Not considering the combined effects of environmental factors (e.g., high temperature + high humidity)
Ignoring the impact of vibration and motion on usability in mobile scenarios

Design Recommendation Keywords
Adaptability, protectiveness, adjustability, durability, environmental compensation, sensory friendliness, anti-glare, noise reduction, easy to clean

Factor card: Physical Environment
Version: 0.1

factors/where-f-002-social-environment.title: Social Environment
factors/where-f-002-social-environment.content:
Definition
The non-physical social conditions surrounding the use of a product or service: the sociocultural atmosphere, interpersonal networks, social norms, discrimination and prejudice, and community support systems.
Why It Matters
The social environment affects whether users feel accepted and safe, and whether they are willing to use a product or service. For example, a social atmosphere marked by bias or discrimination may lead some groups to avoid a technically usable product because of the psychological burden involved. Considering the social environment helps design solutions that promote inclusion, reduce stigmatization, and earn trust across different social groups.
Related Standards and References

UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) Article 8: awareness-raising and combating stereotypes
Anti-discrimination legislation in various countries (e.g., ADA Titles II and III in the US, the EU Equal Treatment Directives)
Social capital theory
Inclusion indices (e.g., the inclusiveness dimensions of the Social Progress Index)
UNESCO guidance on education and social inclusion

Suggested Quantification Methods

Perceived safety: measured through surveys of users’ sense of safety and degree of being respected in specific situations
Discrimination incident reporting rate: complaints or incident records in usage scenarios
Degree of community support: e.g., availability of user organizations and peer support
Alignment with social norms: whether the product conforms to or challenges mainstream social expectations (assessed via focus groups)
Data sources: social surveys, third-party oversight reports, user interviews, social media sentiment analysis

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: content moderation policies on social media platforms, algorithmic bias audits, anonymous options, reporting mechanisms
Industrial design: whether workplace tools account for acceptance across genders and populations, avoiding reinforcement of stereotypes
Architectural design: whether public-space design encourages interaction across groups, avoiding segregating designs (e.g., “poor doors”)
Interior design: whether shared living layouts encourage socializing without intruding on privacy
Graphic design: whether advertising and media represent different groups in diverse and respectful ways
Fashion design: whether styles accommodate the identity-expression needs of different cultures, avoiding cultural appropriation or offense

Common Pitfalls and Blind Spots

Treating technical usability as equivalent to social usability
Overlooking how microaggressions or implicit bias can be transmitted through design
Considering only primary user groups and ignoring the discomfort of marginalized groups in specific situations
Ignoring regional differences in social norms in global products, leading to offense or inapplicability
Designing “neutrally” while actually defaulting to the dominant group’s perspective

Design Recommendation Keywords
Social safety, inclusive representation, bias audits, participatory accessibility, respectful language, cultural sensitivity, empowerment design, low barriers, community co-creation

Factor card: Social Environment
Version: 0.1

factors/where-f-003-spatial-accessibilit.title: Spatial Accessibility
factors/where-f-003-spatial-accessibilit.content:
Definition
The physical barriers users face in reaching, entering, and using a physical space or destination, including distance, path slope, steps, door width, and clearance height.
Why It Matters

Geographic barriers can completely block some users from a product or service
Older adults, people with disabilities, and the temporarily injured are more sensitive to accessibility
Poor accessibility widens social exclusion

Quantification Criteria

Path width: clear passage width (wheelchairs require ≥810mm)
Slope: maximum permitted slope (e.g., 1:12)
Step count: whether alternatives (ramps, elevators) are available
Distance: walking distance and time from transit hubs to the destination

Design Guidelines

Provide accessible routes (ramps, elevators, handrails)
Locate key facilities on lower floors or in easily reached positions
Consider multi-modal access (bus, subway, bicycle)
Provide remote alternatives (e.g., online services, delivery)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainConsiderationsArchitectural designEntrance ramps, elevators, accessible restrooms, tactile pavingUrban planningAccessible sidewalks, reachable public transit stopsRetail spacesMobility scooter aisles, stroller parking, step-free entrancesPublic servicesRemote transaction handling, mobile service vehicles, home-visit services
Related Standards

ADA Standards for Accessible Design
EN 17210: accessibility of buildings
GB 50763-2012: accessibility design code


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Especially important for physical facilities)

factors/where-f-004-resource-availabilit.title: Resource Availability
factors/where-f-004-resource-availabilit.content:
Definition
Whether users can obtain the supporting resources needed while using a product or service, including electricity, water, fuel, cleaning tools, consumable materials, and human assistance.
Why It Matters

Resource shortages directly block some functions (e.g., charging, printing, drying)
Resource constraints are more severe in low-income areas or disaster environments
Some assistive functions depend on dedicated resources (e.g., a braille printer needs paper and power)

Quantification Criteria

Energy: stability of the power supply (outage frequency, voltage fluctuation), gas supply
Water: ease of access to clean water, water quality
Time: waiting or preparation time required to obtain resources
Cost: how well the unit cost of resources matches users’ ability to pay
Substitutability: whether degraded-function or alternative options exist when resources are unavailable

Design Guidelines

Ensure core functions require no scarce resources (e.g., offline capability)
Label resource requirements clearly (e.g., “requires a printer”, “needs power”)
Provide resource alternatives (e.g., disposable batteries instead of charging, handwriting instead of printing)
Optimize resource consumption (power-saving mode, water-saving mode)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainExample resourcesDigital productsElectricity, network bandwidth, storage spaceMedical devicesConsumables (needles, filters), power, water for sterilizationEducational productsPrinted textbooks, whiteboards, projectorsEveryday servicesClean water, paper towels, charging facilities, packaging materials
Related Standards

None specific; context-dependent


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (Scores high in specific scenarios)

factors/where-f-005-economic-environment.title: Economic Environment
factors/where-f-005-economic-environment.content:
Definition
The economic conditions surrounding the use of a product or service, including users’ financial capacity, consumption levels, economic uncertainty, cost tolerance, and the level of economic development in their region — macro- and micro-economic factors alike.
Why It Matters
The economic environment directly affects whether users can obtain, purchase, and keep using a product or service. Even a highly inclusive design still presents a barrier if users cannot afford it or if the local economy cannot support the required infrastructure. Considering the economic environment helps design solutions that are economically accessible, cost-effective, and adaptable to different economic conditions.
Related Standards and References

World Bank income classifications (low, lower-middle, upper-middle, high income)
National poverty lines and minimum living-cost standards
Purchasing power parity (PPP)
The poverty-reduction and inequality targets within the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Consumer protection laws and price regulation in various countries

Suggested Quantification Methods

User level: disposable income, Engel coefficient, whether below the poverty line
Regional level: GDP per capita, economic growth rate, unemployment rate, Gini coefficient
Affordability measures: the maximum users would pay for a specific feature (WTP), tolerance of total cost of ownership (TCO)
Economic vulnerability indices: e.g., income volatility, savings rate, debt levels
Data sources: household surveys, World Bank Open Data, national statistics offices, consumer research

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: low-price or free tiers, data-traffic optimization, support for older devices, offline features that reduce network-dependence costs
Industrial design: material substitution to cut costs, modular design for repairability, process choices suited to local manufacturing capability
Architectural design: local materials, simplified construction methods, phased accessibility retrofits
Interior design: furniture rental or sharing models, multifunctional furniture that reduces repeat purchases
Graphic design: double-sided printing, standardized sizes to reduce waste, digital distribution replacing print
Fashion design: durable design that lengthens replacement cycles, easy-care materials that lower maintenance costs, basic styles covering the mass market

Common Pitfalls and Blind Spots

Assuming target users have similar economic means
Considering only purchase price while ignoring the total cost of use, maintenance, and upgrades
Over-simplifying features in low-income regions, producing “cheap but hard to use” products
Ignoring the impact of economic volatility on long-term availability (e.g., inflation raising costs)
Equating “economically accessible” with “low quality”, ignoring cost-effectiveness achieved through innovation

Design Recommendation Keywords
Economic accessibility, cost-effectiveness, total cost of ownership, tiered pricing, lifecycle cost, local production, repair-friendly, sharing economy, essential functions first

Factor card: Economic Environment

factors/where-f-006-emergency-response.title: Emergency Response
factors/where-f-006-emergency-response.content:
Definition
Users’ ability to use a product or service — and their special needs — during emergencies (e.g., medical crises, fires, natural disasters, safety threats).
Why It Matters

In emergencies users’ cognitive load surges, time is critical, and operating ability is impaired
Routine interaction flows may not meet rapid-response needs
Inclusive design must consider accessibility in vulnerable states

Quantification Criteria

Activation time: the time window from recognizing the emergency to initiating a call for help
Operation complexity: the minimum number of actions an emergency call requires (ideally 1 step)
Accessibility features: whether it can be triggered by voice, a button press, or automatically by environmental sensors
Fault tolerance: the ability to cancel or undo after a false trigger (so accidental activation doesn’t delay real help)

Design Guidelines

Provide a one-touch SOS feature, always accessible (even from the lock screen)
Drastically simplify the emergency flow, avoiding multi-step confirmations (while still offering mis-tap cancellation)
Support multi-channel triggering (voice, gesture, button, automatic detection)
Provide clear emergency-state confirmation and feedback (help called, location shared)
Assume users may be in a panic; design foolproof

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainEmergency feature examplesMobile devicesLock-screen emergency call, fall detection with automatic SOSAutomotiveEmergency braking, one-touch rescue callSmart homeAutomatic fire/gas alarms with notification of emergency contactsWearablesMedical emergency button, abnormal heart-rate alerts
Related Standards

Local emergency call service standards (e.g., 110/120/911)
Emergency-communication requirements in international accessibility standards (e.g., TIA-603)
Product safety certification requirements


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Life-safety related)

factors/where-f-007-usage-context.title: Usage Context
factors/where-f-007-usage-context.content:
Definition
The specific situational conditions under which a product or service is used, including the user’s posture (sitting, standing, walking), one-handed vs two-handed operation, whether on the move, whether attention is focused, whether other tasks are being performed simultaneously (multitasking), the degree of time pressure, and the frequency and duration of use.
Why It Matters
Usage context directly affects users’ perception, operation, and cognitive load. For example, using a phone while walking requires larger touch targets and more concise information; one-handed operation requires easily reachable controls; highly distracting situations require more salient feedback and lower cognitive load. Considering usage context helps design products and services that remain usable, safe, and efficient under real-world conditions.
Subtypes and Specific Dimensions
Posture and hand availability

Sitting / standing / walking / lying / crouching; one-handed / two-handed / no-handed operation; moving / stationary; vibration / unstable platforms

Attention and cognitive load

Focused / distracted / multitasking; time pressure; competition for cognitive resources; situationally increased cognitive load

Sensory environment

Lighting (bright / dim / glare), acoustics (noisy / quiet / echoing), tactile conditions (gloves / wet hands / dirty hands)

Social and privacy context

Alone / in company / observed; public / semi-public / private spaces; social pressure

Situational capability limits

B1 cross-reference reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, benchmarked against Microsoft Inclusive Design and WHO ICF d4/d5-d6)

Situational limitations: not an inherent deficit of the user, but a temporary functional restriction caused by the situation

Visual restriction: screen invisible in bright light, night-driving glare, wearing sunglasses or a helmet
Auditory restriction: speech inaudible in noisy environments, no audio playback allowed in quiet venues, wearing noise-cancelling headphones
Motor restriction: one-handed operation (holding a child / carrying heavy loads / an injured arm / gripping a handrail), wearing gloves or a face mask, confined spaces
Cognitive restriction: reduced processing capacity under pressure, distraction, multitasking, fatigue, or acute stress

Design implication: situational limitations overlap heavily with permanent disabilities in interaction requirements. A unified “situation-adaptation mode” can serve both groups at once.
Mobility and travel scenarios

B1 cross-reference reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, benchmarked against WHO ICF d4)


Walking / wheelchair / crutches / walker: device use while moving
Public transport (subway / bus / airplane): space constraints, vibration, noise, standing / crowding
Driving / cycling: hands-free operation, voice control, head-up displays, minimal glance time
Cross-modal transitions: seamless experience across walking → subway → transfers (account / progress / settings sync)

Private and sensitive-task scenarios

B1 cross-reference reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, benchmarked against WHO ICF d5-d6 self-care and domestic life)


Toilet / changing / bathing: waterproofing, slip resistance, easy cleaning, privacy protection
Medical / medication / monitoring: privacy, accuracy, reminders, data logging
Finance / legal / identity verification: security, shoulder-surfing protection, audit trails
Menstruation / incontinence / stoma care: discretion, easy access, leak prevention, freedom from embarrassment

Related Standards and References

ISO 9241-210: human-centred design (considering the usage context)
“Usage context analysis” in human factors engineering
Distracted-driving research in driving safety standards
Mobile interaction guidelines (e.g., Android Auto, Apple CarPlay)
Task analysis methods (e.g., HTA, CTA)

Suggested Quantification Methods

Posture classification: proportions of sitting, standing, walking, lying, etc.
Hand availability: assessment of one-handed operation feasibility (e.g., degrees of hand freedom)
Attention load: secondary-task reaction time, subjective distraction ratings
Time pressure: available completion time, deadline urgency scores
Frequency and duration of use: sessions per day, average session length
Data sources: context observation, wearable sensors, log analysis, user interviews

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: driving mode, one-handed interfaces, large-font options, voice control, fewer interaction steps
Industrial design: one-handed tools, non-slip grips, heights usable while standing, quick interfaces
Architectural design: clear signage in emergencies, handrail heights adapted to different postures, seating design in waiting areas
Interior design: bedside switches within easy reach, height-zoned kitchen worktops, living-room seating with convenient side access
Graphic design: fast readability of outdoor ads, concise messaging on vehicle ads, reading distances for exhibition panels
Fashion design: pocket placement for easy access, easy-pull zipper design, cuts that don’t restrict movement

Common Pitfalls and Blind Spots

Considering only the ideal, seated, focused usage situation
Ignoring dynamic changes in usage context (e.g., transitions from sitting to walking)
Looking only at average situations and ignoring edge or high-risk ones (e.g., emergencies)
Not accounting for competition for cognitive resources in multitasking scenarios
Designing for “static use” without considering movement or unstable platforms

Design Recommendation Keywords
Situation adaptation, one-handed operation, postural freedom, attention-friendly, time flexibility, multitask-compatible, emergency salience, mobile-optimized

Factor card: Usage Context
Version: 3.1 (B1 reinforcement: situational capability limits / mobility / private-task scenarios)

factors/where-f-008-shared-public-use.title: Shared & Public Use Context
factors/where-f-008-shared-public-use.content:
Definition
The user is not the sole user of the product/space but is situated in a multi-person shared or public setting. Core dimensions include:

Synchronous sharing: multiple people using it at the same time (home TV, meeting-room display, public self-service kiosk)
Asynchronous sharing: multiple people taking turns (family tablet, shared office desks, library computers)
Bystanders / being observed: the act of use can be seen/heard by others (reading in public, using a phone on the subway, calls in an open-plan office)
Account/configuration sharing: family shared accounts, team shared workspaces, multi-user logins on a device

Distinguishing it from other factors:

WHERE-F-007 (Usage Context) focuses on the physical/social environment of a single user
WHICH-F-008 (Interaction Mode Preference) focuses on the user’s subjective preference for working alone vs collaboratively
This factor focuses on the constraints that the objective presence of non-target users places on privacy, usability, and safety

Why It Matters

Family-shared devices: children’s accidental purchases, private content seen by family members, personalized recommendations interfering with one another
Public self-service kiosks: passwords entered under onlookers’ eyes, residual traces of operation, time pressure (queues)
Open-plan offices: screen content exposure, overheard calls, meeting interruptions
Public transit / outdoors: screen reflections, noise interference, device theft risk

Design Response (both: alternatives + choice space)
Constraint components → provide alternatives

Privacy mode: screen privacy filters, directional audio, automatic clearing of traces
Guest/temporary mode: no history saved, no pollution of the main account’s recommendations
Lock screen / fast account switching: hide sensitive content with a single action

Preference/context components → provide choice space

Personalization isolation on shared devices: multi-user profiles, fingerprint/face fast switching
Configurable “visibility”: work material visible only to colleagues, personal photos only to family
Public-setting adaptation: automatically enable privacy mode when public Wi-Fi/Bluetooth beacons are detected

Cross-Domain Mapping






























DomainExclusion exampleInclusion exampleDigital productsMuddled recommendations on family-shared accounts, screens peeked at in publicMulti-user profiles, guest mode, privacy screenIndustrial designShared tools with no user identification, public facilities with no privacy designMulti-user RFID identification, separated public seatingArchitectural designOpen-plan offices with no privacy zones, large gaps in public toilet stallsPhone booths/focus pods, all-gender restrooms, acoustic partitionsFashion designFitting rooms with no hooks or badly placed mirrors, shared changing roomsIndividual fitting rooms, lockable lockers, privacy curtains
Measurement Dimensions

Completeness of multi-user profiles (whether independent data isolation is supported)
Availability of guest/privacy mode
Mitigations for observation risk (privacy filters, directional audio, automatic clearing)

Related Standards and References

UD7 supplementary principle P8 (Community)
WHO ICF d7 (interpersonal interactions) and d9 (education and work)
Pending WP-C linkage: ISO 9241-210 usage context, related privacy standards

B1 Cross-Reference Note
This factor was added by the INCL-XREF-001 GAP-2 determination: none of the 5 benchmark frameworks has a structured factor for “shared/public use context.”

factors/where-f-009-assisted-use-context.title: Assisted Use Context
factors/where-f-009-assisted-use-context.content:
Definition
Situations in which, while the user operates a product/space, a third-party assistant (caregiver, family member, professional care worker, sign-language interpreter, translator, guide dog, etc.) is present, collaborates, or operates on the user’s behalf. Core dimensions include:

Type of assistance:

Physical assistance (pushing a wheelchair, operating equipment on the user’s behalf, physical transfers)
Sensory assistance (sign-language interpretation, visual guidance, reading screen content aloud)
Cognitive assistance (decision support, process guidance, memory prompts, emotional reassurance)
Technical assistance (configuring accounts on the user’s behalf, operating complex settings, troubleshooting)


Assistance relationship:

Professional care workers / agency services (trained, with defined responsibility boundaries)
Informal caregivers (family/friends: complex emotional relationships, ambiguous permissions)
Community volunteers / peer support
Assistance animals / smart assistive devices



Distinguishing it from other factors:

WHO-F-001/003/009: the user’s own ability state
WHERE-F-007/008: the objective environment / shared settings
This factor focuses on the interaction-design needs arising from a third party actively intervening in the usage process (three-way interaction: user–assistant–system)

Why It Matters

When a caregiver operates a screen reader on the user’s behalf, the UI must support an “observer’s view” (high contrast, large font, clear status indication)
When family members configure a smart home, it needs “delegated permission management” (tiered authorization, audit logs)
When a nurse operates medical equipment, it needs dual “professional mode / home mode” interfaces
When a sign-language interpreter joins a video meeting, it needs a “multi-window layout” (presenter/interpreter/captions on one screen)
When a guardian manages a child’s or elder’s device, it needs a “guardian dashboard” (usage time, content filtering, location tracking)

Design Response (both: alternatives + choice space)
Constraint/ability components → provide alternatives

Proxy-operation interface: a separate entry point for the assistant (web admin console, mobile control app)
Three-way synchronized view: state sync between the main user interface and the assistant’s interface (without leaking privacy)
Tiered permissions: read-only / assisted operation / full delegation / emergency takeover, revocable by the user at any time

Preference/relationship components → provide choice space

Autonomy-preservation mechanism: the user can set “request help only when I cannot complete it” vs “assistant always leads”
Privacy-boundary configuration: what the assistant can see is configurable (task progress only / full content / anomaly alerts only)
Relationship-mode presets: professional care-worker mode (strict permissions/auditing) vs family mode (loose/emotion-first)

Cross-Domain Mapping






























DomainExclusion exampleInclusion exampleDigital productsNo delegated permissions; the assistant can only share the account passwordTiered delegated permissions, assistant-only dashboard, operation audit logsIndustrial designMedical equipment with professional mode only; family cannot assistProfessional/home dual modes, physical keys coexisting with digital authorizationArchitectural designNo companion space; no caregiver position in restroomsCompanion beds, caregiver-accessible restrooms, companion areas in waiting roomsFashion designCannot dress/undress independently; assisted dressing is difficultMagnetic closures/Velcro, wide-opening designs, assisted-dressing labels
Measurement Dimensions

Tiering completeness of the delegated-permission system
Usability and latency of the three-way synchronized view
Configurability of privacy boundaries
Assistant onboarding time / error rate

Related Standards and References

WHO ICF e3 support and relationships (human assistance)
Pending WP-C linkage: IEC 60601 usability of medical electrical equipment, ISO 21542 built-environment accessibility (companion spaces)

B1 Cross-Reference Note
This factor was added by the INCL-XREF-001 GAP-5 determination: ICF e3 explicitly lists “human assistance”, while the other 4 benchmarks have no such structured factor.

factors/which-f-001-information-density-.title: Information Density Preference
factors/which-f-001-information-density-.content:
Definition
The user’s degree of preference for, and tolerance range of, the amount of information and level of detail presented at once.
Why It Matters

Information overload → cognitive load ↑, anxiety ↑
Too little information → efficiency ↓, distrust ↑
Needs differ greatly across scenarios (e.g., data analysts vs. ordinary users)

Quantification Criteria

Measurement methods: eye tracking (fixation duration, saccade paths), user self-assessment (preference scales)
