Metrics: on-screen element density, text line-height density, data-point density
Reference thresholds: general web pages are advised to keep font size ≥ 16px and line spacing ≥ 1.5

Design Guidelines

Provide a “compact mode” / “detailed mode” toggle
Layer information: summary → detail (collapse/expand)
Let users customize their dashboard (control over what is displayed)
Default density set to “medium”, with an entry point for adjustment

Cross-Domain Manifestations






























DomainLow-density preferenceHigh-density preferenceDigital productsMinimalist, generous whitespace, less is moreData-dense, everything at a glance, multi-panelIndustrial designSimplified interfaces, key controls highlightedMultifunction panels, parameters displayed centrallyArchitectural designOpen space, minimalist decorationMultifunction composite, compact spaceFashion designClean styles, minimal ornamentationLayered combinations, abundant accessories
Related Standards

WCAG 1.4.4: Resize Text (without breaking layout)
Nielsen Norman Group: balancing information density and readability


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (An extremely common preference difference)

factors/which-f-002-exploration-depth-pr.title: Exploration Depth Preference
factors/which-f-002-exploration-depth-pr.content:
Definition
Whether users tend toward a quick overview or an in-depth examination when exploring content or features.
Why It Matters

Accommodating different users’ exploration modes reduces churn
Affects interface navigation structure design (flat vs hierarchical)

Quantification Criteria

Measurement methods: user behavior analytics (page-visit depth, feature usage rates)
Metrics: average time on page, diversity of feature usage
Preference segments: typically divided into “quick finders” and “deep researchers”

Design Guidelines

Provide a “quick start” path (default for newcomers)
Also provide entry points to “advanced settings” or “expert mode”
Navigation supports multi-level access (breadcrumbs, quick back)
Give equal weight to search and browsing

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Digital products: onboarding tutorials vs advanced manuals, prominence of search
Knowledge bases: summary version vs full version, skimming vs detailed study
Retail spaces: curated displays vs detailed exploration areas
Clothing selection: quick outfit recommendations vs detailed inspection of materials and workmanship

Related Standards

None specifically; derived from user research segmentation


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (Important for content-intensive products)

factors/which-f-003-control-preference.title: Control Preference
factors/which-f-003-control-preference.content:
Definition
The user’s preference, when completing a task, for how much autonomous control they have over the process versus how much is automated.
Why It Matters

Too little sense of control → helplessness, distrust
Too much control burden → heavy load, low efficiency
Affects adoption of new technology (e.g., acceptance of automated driving)

Quantification Criteria

Measurement methods: survey scales (automation acceptance, willingness to intervene manually)
Metrics: how often users actually use automated vs manual features
Tolerance threshold: the proportion of control users are willing to give up in certain tasks

Design Guidelines

Offer adjustable levels of automation (e.g., “fully automatic”, “semi-automatic”, “manual”)
Allow users to override system decisions
Provide undo mechanisms to increase the sense of safety
Make the current system state and expected behavior explicit
Consistent help: a fixed help entry point, a unified help-content structure, context-sensitive help coexisting with global help, and help that can be summoned at any time without interrupting the main flow (implements WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.6; guideline-layer implementation via WP-E)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Digital products: accepting/rejecting autofill suggestions, transparency of recommendation algorithms
Industrial equipment: manual override, semi-automatic mode, fully automatic mode
Smart buildings: automatic environmental adjustment + manual control panels
Clothing: adjustable parts (buttons, zippers, straps) vs one-step dressing

Related Standards

ISO 9241-110: controllability principle
Parasuraman et al.’s theory of trust and automation
WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.6: Consistent Help


Factor card: Control Preference
Version: 3.1 (B1 reinforcement: consistent-help guideline points)

factors/which-f-004-social-visibility-pr.title: Social Visibility Preference
factors/which-f-004-social-visibility-pr.content:
Basic Definition
Users’ preference for how much personal information, activity status, and online presence they expose during social interactions.
Why It Matters

Privacy concerns are one of the leading exclusion factors
Poorly configured social-visibility settings can drive user churn
Forced social features (e.g., real-name policies) can exclude users who prefer anonymity

Quantification Criteria

Measurement methods: surveys of privacy-settings usage, selection rates of visibility options
Metric: the proportion of users who change default privacy settings
Sensitivity tiers: different sensitivity levels for personal information, location, activity, friend lists, and so on

Design Guidelines

Provide fine-grained visibility controls (independent settings per item of information and per feature)
Default to the strictest privacy options
Clearly indicate the current visibility state
Contextual presets (e.g., “friends only”, “work contacts only”)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

Social apps: who can see my posts and online status
Wearables: whether workout achievements are shared to social networks
Smart home: whether household activity logs are shared with visitors
Fashion design: choices over degree of exposure (body coverage, fitted vs. loose)

Related Standards

Privacy regulations such as GDPR and CCPA
ISO/IEC 27701: Privacy information management systems


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (core of privacy protection)

factors/which-f-005-aesthetic-style-pref.title: Aesthetic Style Preference
factors/which-f-005-aesthetic-style-pref.content:
Basic Definition
Users’ preferences in visual and sensory presentation style, including color, shape, material, animation density, sound tonality, and more.
Why It Matters

Aesthetics are highly subjective; forcing a single style lowers user comfort and sense of identification
Preferences differ widely across industries and cultural backgrounds
Offering style choices boosts brand affinity and user stickiness

Quantification Criteria

Measurement methods: style-preference questionnaires, eye-tracking heatmaps, dwell time, theme-usage statistics
Dimensions: minimal vs. rich, cool vs. warm tones, modern vs. traditional, bold vs. soft
Consistency: whether a user’s preference for a single style is consistent across platforms

Design Guidelines

Offer multiple official themes (dark/light, high-contrast/soft, dynamic/static)
Allow customization (colors, fonts, icon sets)
Keep core feature locations stable across style switches (reducing relearning cost)
The default style should be broadly acceptable (neutral, highly readable)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainStyle dimensionsDigital productsflat vs. skeuomorphic, neon glow vs. understated eleganceIndustrial designstreamlined vs. geometric and angular, metal vs. woodArchitectural designminimalism vs. ornamental richness, modern vs. traditionalFashion designstreetwear, business formal, anime-inspired, retro
Related Standards

No mandatory standards; follow brand guidelines and user research


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (especially important for consumer products)

factors/which-f-006-input-method-prefere.title: Input Method Preference
factors/which-f-006-input-method-prefere.content:
Basic Definition
The input modalities users prefer for interacting with a system — keyboard, mouse, touch, voice, gesture, eye tracking, switch devices, and so on — as well as the strength of these preferences and how the modalities are combined.
Why It Matters

Users differ widely in familiarity, comfort, and efficiency across input methods
Physical conditions can rule out certain inputs (e.g., one-handed operation, fine motor control)
Context also affects the best input (voice while driving; keyboard and mouse in the office)
Offering input switching improves accessibility and user satisfaction

Quantification Criteria

Input method usage frequency: share of each modality across tasks
Switching frequency: how often users switch input methods within a single session
Error rate: operational error rate per input method
Satisfaction ratings: comfort and efficiency ratings per input method

Design Guidelines

Support multiple input devices simultaneously without mandating a single method (e.g., keep keyboard shortcuts)
Let users set default input method / device priority
Provide a quick entry point for switching input methods
Support input remapping (e.g., key remapping, custom gestures)
Context awareness: automatically suggest a suitable input (e.g., voice while on the move)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainInput method examplesDesktop softwaremouse, keyboard, trackpad, stylus, voice commandsMobile appstouch, gestures, external keyboards, voice inputGame devicesgamepads, keyboard + mouse, motion controls, VR controllers, steering wheelsIndustrial/medicalswitches, foot pedals, head control, eye tracking, breath control
Related Standards

Platform accessibility frameworks (e.g., UI Automation, AT-SPI)
Standards for alternative input devices (e.g., USB HID)
IEEE 11064: human-computer interaction design principles


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (essential for hardware-interaction products)

factors/which-f-007-feedback-preference.title: Feedback Preference
factors/which-f-007-feedback-preference.content:
Basic Definition
Users’ subjective preferences for the form, intensity, duration, and sensory channel (visual, auditory, tactile) of the system’s responses to their actions.
Why It Matters

Feedback is the foundation of interaction; poorly tuned feedback distracts or gets missed
Needs differ by context (quiet in the office, prominent outdoors)
Users with photosensitive epilepsy or autism need to avoid certain feedback forms

Quantification Criteria

Feedback intensity: alert volume, animation duration, and vibration strength users can accept
Channel preference: ratio of visual / auditory / haptic usage
Interruption tolerance: ratings of how intrusive non-task-related alerts feel
Information density: desired level of feedback detail (confirmation only vs. detailed status)

Design Guidelines

Let users adjust the intensity of each channel or turn specific channels off
Provide silent mode and do-not-disturb mode
Use strong multi-channel feedback for urgent or high-risk states (but keep it configurable)
Design for photosensitivity, sound sensitivity, and other special needs

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainFeedback formsMobile appsalert tones, vibration, visual toasts, status-bar updatesDesktop softwaresound cues, taskbar flashing, balloon notificationsIndustrial controlindicator lights, buzzers, haptic feedback (force-feedback controllers)Wearablesvibration patterns, lights, voice feedback
Related Standards

WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1: Timing Adjustable
Flicker and sound requirements in accessibility guidelines


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (broad impact across interactive products)

factors/which-f-008-interaction-mode-pre.title: Interaction Mode Preference
factors/which-f-008-interaction-mode-pre.content:
Basic Definition
The interaction styles users prefer when working with a system — direct manipulation (clicking, dragging) vs. command-based (typing instructions), gestures, voice, keyboard shortcuts, and so on.
Why It Matters

Users differ widely in proficiency and comfort across interaction modes
Task context also shapes the best mode (e.g., voice suits driving)
Offering multiple interaction modes improves both efficiency and accessibility

Quantification Criteria

Usage frequency: actual share of use of each mode
Error rate: operational error rate within a mode
Task completion time: average time to complete the same task in different modes
Learning curve: time needed to master a new mode

Design Guidelines

Support multiple interaction modes at once (mouse, touch, keyboard, voice)
Let users set a default interaction mode
Do not force mode switches (e.g., keep right-click menus on touch devices)
Provide shortcuts for switching modes

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainMode examplesDesktop softwaremenu navigation, keyboard shortcuts, command line, drag and dropMobile appstouch gestures, voice input, physical buttonsSmart homeapp control, voice assistants, physical switches, automation scenesGamingkeyboard + mouse, gamepads, motion controls, touchscreens
Related Standards

No unified standard; follow platform conventions (iOS HIG, Material Design)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (multimodal interaction products)

factors/which-f-009-notification-prefere.title: Notification Preference
factors/which-f-009-notification-prefere.content:
Basic Definition
Users’ need for control over which messages a system pushes to them, when, through which channels, and at what importance. Notifications are a potential source of interruption, and preferences vary enormously.
Why It Matters

Ill-judged pushes cause anxiety, loss of focus, and uninstalls
Some users need real-time notifications (e.g., executives, support staff) while others need to concentrate
Notification fatigue lowers response rates to important messages

Quantification Criteria

Notification frequency: how many notifications per day / per hour users want to receive
Time windows: periods during which pushes are allowed (e.g., work hours only)
Channel choice: preferred push channels (push, email, SMS, in-app messages)
Priority threshold: only high-priority messages may interrupt strongly

Design Guidelines

Provide fine-grained controls (by type, sender, urgency)
Default to conservative settings (critical notifications only)
Let users pause all notifications (focus mode)
Respect time zones and daily-rhythm differences

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainNotification scenariosSocial appsmentions, direct messages, event remindersProductivity toolstask deadlines, schedule changes, collaboration requestsE-commerceorder status, price drops, promotionsSmart homesecurity alarms, device faults, energy-saving reminders
Related Standards

Platform notification policies (e.g., iOS notification grouping, Android Do Not Disturb)
GDPR restrictions on marketing communications


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (key to retention for UGC/social products)

factors/who-f-001-physical-ability.title: Physical & Cognitive Ability
factors/who-f-001-physical-ability.content:
Definition
Users’ physiological and neurological capabilities in perception, motor function, and cognition, including ability levels and limitations across vision, hearing, touch, balance, coordination, strength, endurance, memory, attention, executive function, and more.
Why It Matters
Variation in physical ability is a core consideration of inclusive design. Ignoring different ability levels makes products or services unusable or hard to use for particular user groups, creating exclusion. Accounting for physical ability leads to more broadly usable solutions — meeting the needs of people with disabilities while improving the experience for everyone (the spillover effect).
Subtypes and Specific Ability Dimensions
Visual ability

Visual acuity (LogMAR/Snellen), visual field, color vision, contrast sensitivity, light sensitivity, dark adaptation

Auditory ability

Hearing thresholds (decibels), speech-recognition resolution, sound localization, auditory processing speed

Touch and proprioception

Tactile thresholds (monofilament testing), vibration sense, temperature sense, proprioceptive precision

Speech production

Articulation clarity, speech-rate control, glottal control, motor control of the articulators
Related conditions: dysarthria, aphasia, post-laryngeal surgery, laryngectomy
Design responses: alternatives to voice input (text/gesture/eye tracking), authentication paths that do not depend on speech

Motor ability

Fine motor: finger dexterity, pinch strength, precision of manipulation
Gross motor: range of motion, strength, endurance, coordination, balance
Temporary/situational limitations: an arm in a cast, holding a baby, operating with gloves on, one-handed use

Cognition and neurological function

Attention: sustained, selective, and divided attention
Memory: working-memory capacity, short-term/long-term memory, prospective memory
Executive function: planning, inhibitory control, task switching, decision-making
Processing speed: reaction time, speed of information extraction
Neurodiversity: ADHD, autism spectrum, dyslexia, developmental coordination disorder

Temporary and Situational Ability Limitations

B1 cross-contrast reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, contrasted with Microsoft Inclusive Design)

Ability limitations are not only permanent:

Temporary: bone fractures, eye infections, laryngitis, post-surgical recovery, medication side effects
Situational: bright light/dark environments, noisy/quiet environments, one-handed operation (holding a child/carrying shopping bags), wearing gloves/masks, exercising/driving, stress/fatigue

Design implication: permanent, temporary, and situational limitations overlap heavily at the interaction level (one-handed mode, voice control, large touch targets, etc.). Design should cover all three, rather than targeting permanent disability alone.
Age-Related Combined Decline Across Multiple Abilities

B1 cross-contrast reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, contrasted with the Cambridge EDC exclusion calculator)

Aging often brings a combined, progressive decline across multiple dimensions of ability:

declining vision + degraded fine motor control + slower processing + reduced working-memory capacity
not an accumulation of separate impairments but a systematic rightward shift of capability curves
design must consider “combinations of abilities” rather than single-dimension thresholds

Related Standards and References

WCAG 2.1/2.2: perceivable and operable principles (contrast, keyboard accessibility, sufficient time, etc.)
ISO 21542: accessibility requirements in the built environment (corridor widths, ramp gradients, handrail heights, etc.)
ANSI/HFES 100-2007: human factors engineering of computer workstations
ISO 9999: classification of assistive products
Human factors databases: ANSUR II, NHANES anthropometric data

Suggested Quantification Methods

Perceptual ability: minimum detectable stimulus thresholds (e.g., visual acuity in LogMAR, hearing in decibels), contrast sensitivity
Motor ability: range of motion (joint angles), strength measurement (newtons), fine motor control (peak velocity, trajectory deviation)
Cognitive ability: reaction time, working-memory capacity (e.g., digit span), executive-function tests (e.g., the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test)
Functional assessment: standard scales (e.g., PROMIS, WHODAS 2.0) or task completion rates, error rates, subjective workload (NASA-TLX)
Data sources: disability statistics (e.g., US CDC, the WHO World Report on Disability), anthropometric percentile data

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: screen reader compatibility, touch target sizes, voice input, adjustable fonts and spacing, reduced-motion options
Industrial design: handle dimensions and shapes, operating-force requirements, display height and angle, misuse prevention
Architectural design: door widths, ramp gradients, handrail heights and extensions, stair riser heights, reachability of elevator buttons
Interior design: adjustable furniture, corridor widths, lighting uniformity and glare control, sound-dampening materials
Graphic design: type size and readability, color contrast, clarity of information hierarchy, avoiding color-only information
Fashion design: ease of dressing (fastener types, opening sizes), cuts that do not restrict movement, sensory-friendly fabrics, ease of care

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Considering only extreme disabilities (e.g., blindness, paralysis) and overlooking mild-to-moderate ability variations
Assuming all older adults lose abilities uniformly, ignoring individual differences
Focusing only on permanent disability and overlooking temporary or situational ability limitations (holding a baby, vision restricted by bright light)
Over-relying on visual or auditory feedback with no multi-sensory redundancy
Designing for an “average user”, excluding users at the margins

Design Recommendation Keywords
Adjustable, multi-sensory feedback, error tolerance, minimal physical effort, reduced cognitive load, consistency, predictability, assistive-technology compatibility

Factor card: Physical Ability
Version: 3.1 (B1 reinforcement: speech production / touch / temporary / situational / age-related combined decline)

factors/who-f-002-demographics.title: Demographics
factors/who-f-002-demographics.content:
Definition
The basic statistical characteristics of a user population, including age, gender, income level, education, occupation, household structure, geographic distribution, and more. These characteristics shape usage needs, ability distributions, and behavior patterns.
Why It Matters
Different population groups differ markedly in abilities, preferences, usage contexts, and economic capacity. Ignoring demographic characteristics can produce designs that fail to match the target users’ actual needs or that over-focus on a minority group. Considering demographics helps target user groups precisely, forecast the scale of demand, and design products or services with better market fit.
Related Standards and References

United Nations demographic classification standards
National census and social survey methodologies (e.g., the US ACS, Eurostat)
World Bank data classifications (income level, education level)
Market research association guidelines (e.g., ESOMAR)
ISO 20252: Market, opinion and social research

Suggested Quantification Methods

Age distribution: mean age, median, share of age groups (e.g., 0-14, 15-64, 65+)
Gender ratios: male/female ratio, recognition rate of non-binary gender identities
Education level: shares with less than secondary, with secondary, and with tertiary education or above
Income level: disposable income per capita, share below the poverty line, Engel coefficient
Geographic distribution: urban/rural ratio, regional development level indices
Data sources: official statistical offices, World Bank open data, UN data, market research reports

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: interaction complexity designed per age group (e.g., kids’ modes, simplified interfaces for older adults), gender-specific feature needs, regional language and payment-method adaptation
Industrial design: tool sizes scaled to different body proportions; usage contexts that reflect occupational traits (construction worker vs. office worker)
Architectural design: accessible design for aging communities, density and functional zoning of student housing, affordable housing for low-income groups
Interior design: furniture sized to anthropometric percentile data; storage designed around the number of household members
Graphic design: ad targeting, visual styles matched to the target aesthetic group, information density matched to reading habits
Fashion design: size systems covering different body types, styles matched to occupation and lifestyle, price points matched to spending tiers

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Treating the user population as a homogeneous whole, ignoring internal differences
Over-relying on stereotypes (e.g., “all older adults can’t handle technology”)
Overlooking emerging groups (e.g., Gen Z, digital nomads) or migrant populations
Looking only at totals instead of segmented needs (ability variation within a single age band can be enormous)
Ignoring regional development gaps in global products, producing feature overkill or shortfalls

Design Recommendation Keywords
Market segmentation, audience personas, life-cycle stages, accessible price points, cultural sensitivity, regional adaptation, demand forecasting, inclusive pricing

Factor card: Demographics
Version: 0.1

factors/who-f-003-health-status.title: Health Status
factors/who-f-003-health-status.content:
Definition
Users’ physical and mental health states, including chronic conditions, temporary illnesses, allergies, immune-system status, pain levels, fatigue, and sensitivities to particular environments or materials.
Why It Matters
Health status directly affects users’ capability, comfort, and safety. For example, users with respiratory conditions are sensitive to air quality, users with arthritis need low-operating-force designs, and immunocompromised users may avoid touching public surfaces. Considering health status helps design products or services that are safe and comfortable across health states without adding to disease burden.
Subtypes and Specific Dimensions
Chronic conditions

Respiratory (asthma, COPD), cardiovascular, diabetes, neurological (epilepsy, Parkinson’s), autoimmune diseases

Temporary and situational health issues

B1 cross-contrast reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, contrasted with Microsoft Inclusive Design)


Temporary: colds/flu, fracture recovery, post-surgical recovery, medication side effects (drowsiness/blurred vision), pregnancy
Situational: altitude sickness, motion sickness, symptoms triggered by bright light/noise, stress-induced symptom flare-ups

Allergies and sensitivities

Food/drug allergies, contact dermatitis (nickel/latex/fragrance), multiple chemical sensitivity (MCS), electromagnetic hypersensitivity (EHS)

Pain and fatigue

Chronic pain (back pain, arthritis, neuropathic pain), fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, cancer-related fatigue

Urogenital and continence function

B1 cross-contrast reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, contrasted with WHO ICF b6)


urinary/fecal incontinence, urinary frequency/urgency, urinary catheters/ostomy pouches, menstruation- and menopause-related needs
Design implications: bathroom accessibility and trip frequency, ease of removing clothing, tolerance for interrupting long tasks

Mental health

Anxiety disorders, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), obsessive-compulsive disorder, eating disorders
Design implications: tolerance for cognitive load, decision fatigue, tolerance of social pressure, recovery after errors

Age-related multi-system combined changes

B1 cross-contrast reinforcement (INCL-XREF-001, contrasted with the Cambridge EDC exclusion calculator)


Nonlinear, combined decline across body systems: cardiorespiratory endurance + muscle strength + sensory acuity + cognitive processing speed + immune resilience
Comorbidity is the norm: people over 65 carry an average of 2-3 chronic conditions simultaneously
Design implication: modeling a single health condition is insufficient — consider “health combinations” and functional reserve

Related Standards and References

WHO International Classification of Diseases (ICD)
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) definition of “major life activities”
ISO 9999: classification of assistive products (helps interpret health limitations and assistive needs)
National occupational health and safety standards (e.g., OSHA)
Health and safety guidance in ergonomics

Suggested Quantification Methods

Self-reported health scales: e.g., SF-36, EQ-5D, PROMIS
Condition-specific measures: e.g., the Asthma Control Test, pain scales (VAS), fatigue severity scales
Environmental sensitivity testing: reactions to specific chemicals or allergens
Activity-limitation assessment: how much health conditions impede task completion
Data sources: health surveys, clinical records (de-identified), user interviews, health-monitoring device data

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: reduced-cognitive-load options, voice control to cut physical operation, rest reminders, avoiding flashing content to prevent seizures
Industrial design: low-operating-force handles, non-slip grips, easy-to-clean surfaces, reduced vibration transmission
Architectural design: accessible restrooms, ample rest areas, air purification systems, low-VOC materials
Interior design: easy-to-clean surfaces, hypoallergenic materials, adjustable furniture for pain or mobility limits
Graphic design: avoiding high-frequency flicker, large clear type, color choices that work for color-vision deficiency
Fashion design: non-itchy fabrics, good breathability, easy dressing and undressing (e.g., hook-and-loop fasteners instead of buttons), no zippers or designs that reduce pressure points

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Equating health status with disability alone, ignoring temporary or fluctuating health issues
Assuming all users are healthy, designing only for the “worst case” and over-engineering
Ignoring mental-health effects (e.g., how anxiety and depression affect motivation to use)
Not considering that users may need to seek care at any moment or carry medical devices
Focusing on a single condition and missing the complexity of comorbidity

Design Recommendation Keywords
Health safety, low operating force, easy cleaning, environmental friendliness, reduced stimulation, rest reminders, adaptability, accessible hygiene, material safety

Factor card: Health Status
Version: 3.1 (B1 reinforcement: temporary / situational / urogenital / age-related combined decline)

factors/who-f-004-learning-style.title: Learning Style
factors/who-f-004-learning-style.content:
Basic Definition
The ways users tend to receive and process information when learning something new or using a new product. Common types include visual, auditory, read/write, and kinesthetic (the VAK/VARK model), plus deeper cognitive styles (field dependence/independence, reflectivity/impulsivity, etc.).
Why It Matters

Users with different learning styles vary widely in how quickly and how satisfactorily they understand the same instructional material or onboarding flow
Offering multiple learning paths reduces training costs and error rates
Respecting learning-style preferences boosts user confidence and the willingness to keep using the product

Quantification Criteria

VARK questionnaire scores: score distribution across channels (visual, auditory, read/write, kinesthetic)
Learning time: time to mastery under different modes
Test performance: comprehension test scores after different teaching methods
Preference consistency: whether users’ explicit choices among these modes match their implicit behavior

Design Guidelines

Offer multimodal content as options (illustrated text, video, explanations, interactive walkthroughs)
Let guided tutorials switch the learning order on demand (demo → try, or try → hint)
Let users choose a default help mode (video / illustrated text / interactive guidance)
Support pace control: repeat, fast-forward, slow down

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainExamplesSoftware useillustrated help, video tutorials, interactive walkthroughs, text manualsDevice operationpictorial labels, spoken operating cues, hands-on coaching, tactile markersSpatial wayfindingvisualized maps, audio guides, written descriptions, in-situ experienceDressingvideo styling tutorials, illustrated steps, dressing-aid markers
Related Standards

None specific; educational psychology research (e.g., VARK, Kolb’s learning styles)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (important for educational and B2B software)

factors/who-f-005-emotion-motivation.title: Emotion & Motivation
factors/who-f-005-emotion-motivation.content:
Definition
Users’ emotional states while using a product or service, their intrinsic drives, goals, and values, and their subjective experience of using it — including trust, belonging, achievement, frustration, anxiety, and other emotional factors.
Why It Matters
Emotion and motivation directly determine whether users are willing to start using, keep using, and be satisfied with and loyal to a product. Even a functionally usable product gets abandoned when negative emotions (frustration, fear) take over. Considering emotion and motivation helps design products or services that are not just usable but pleasant, empowering, and aligned with users’ values.
Related Standards and References

ISO 9241-210: human-centred design (covering user satisfaction and pleasure)
User experience (UX) models: e.g., the joy-of-use model, the three levels of emotional design (visceral, behavioral, reflective)
Self-Determination Theory: the three basic needs of intrinsic motivation (autonomy, competence, relatedness)
Gamification design principles
Research on brand emotional attachment

Suggested Quantification Methods

Affect measures: rating scales (e.g., PANAS — the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule; SAM — the Self-Assessment Manikin)
Satisfaction scales: e.g., CSAT, NPS, and emotion-related items in the SUS (System Usability Scale)
Motivation measures: intrinsic motivation scales (e.g., adapted versions such as the Sport Motivation Scale)
Behavioral indicators: usage duration and frequency, voluntary referral rates, repurchase rates
Applying depression and anxiety screening tools in specific contexts (e.g., anxiety when using medical devices)
Data sources: user interviews, diary studies, experience sampling method (ESM), behavioral log analysis

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: achievement systems, positive feedback, less shame around errors, a sense of control, social-connection features
Industrial design: comfort and pride during use, smoothness of operation, convenience of maintenance and repair
Architectural design: the calm a space provides, belonging, safety, designs that spark creativity or social interaction
Interior design: the relaxation furniture affords, emotional responses to color and material, a sense of flow through space
Graphic design: emotional resonance of visual communication; how presentation shapes credibility and approachability
Fashion design: self-image satisfaction after dressing, comfort and confidence, a medium for expressing identity

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Focusing only on functional usability and ignoring the emotional experience
Assuming all users share the same emotional triggers
Over-relying on reward mechanics while neglecting the cultivation of intrinsic motivation
Ignoring potential anxiety or trauma triggers in high-pressure or sensitive contexts
Equating “delight” with gamified entertainment rather than context-appropriate positive feeling

Design Recommendation Keywords
Emotional feedback, trust building, sense of empowerment, belonging, positive reinforcement, reduced anxiety, autonomy support, meaning, social connection, pleasantness

Factor card: Emotion & Motivation
Version: 0.1

factors/who-f-006-sensory-preference.title: Sensory Preference
factors/who-f-006-sensory-preference.content:
Definition
Users’ preferences for, sensitivity to, and aversion to sensory stimuli (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory), including their subjective impressions of and physiological reactions to brightness, color, sound, vibration, texture, and other sensory attributes.
Why It Matters
Sensory preferences directly affect users’ comfort, acceptance, and willingness to use. For example, users sensitive to bright light may avoid high-brightness interfaces, and users averse to certain textures may refuse to use specific products. Considering sensory preferences helps design products or services that are sensory-friendly, minimize discomfort, and match users’ subjective experience.
Related Standards and References

WCAG 2.1: guidance on color and contrast (but it does not cover subjective preferences)
ISO 9241-210: human-centred design (covering user comfort)
Sensory evaluation methods: e.g., sensory difference tests, preference tests
Sensory-processing sensitivity models in neuroscience
Industry sensory design guidelines (e.g., automotive interiors, food packaging)

Suggested Quantification Methods

Subjective ratings: Likert scales of liking or discomfort for specific sensory stimuli (e.g., 1-7 from strongly dislike to strongly like)
Physiological measures: responses such as heart-rate variability, skin conductance, and pupil size
Choice tests: asking users to choose between different sensory conditions
Data sources: sensory lab testing, user research, focus groups

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: adjustable color themes, dark mode, adjustable sound feedback, vibration-strength options, reduced flashing/animation options
Industrial design: handle material choices (rubber, metal, wood grain), operating-sound design, product weight and balance
Architectural design: material textures (walls, handrails), control of ambient sound (echo, noise), combinations of natural and artificial light
Interior design: preferences in soft-furnishing materials (fabric, leather), light color-temperature choices, scent management in spaces
Graphic design: color-pairing preferences, use of texture, tactile print effects (e.g., embossing, foil stamping)
Fashion design: fabric hand-feel (cotton, silk, synthetics), fit on the body, tactile comfort of labels and seams

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Assuming one “neutral” sensory design suits everyone
Designing to average preferences and ignoring polarized groups (users who love brightness coexist with users who loathe it)
Ignoring that sensory preferences shift with context, fatigue, or health status
Over-relying on vision or hearing while neglecting other sensory channels (touch, smell)

Design Recommendation Keywords
Sensory adjustability, active feedback, material selection, sound design, tactile friendliness, low-stimulation options, personalized sensory settings, sensory consistency

Factor card: Sensory Preference
Version: 0.1

factors/who-f-007-technical-literacy.title: Technical Literacy
factors/who-f-007-technical-literacy.content:
Definition
Users’ level of knowledge, skill, and experience with technical products or services, including proficiency in operating digital devices, the ability to understand interfaces, the capacity to learn new systems, and adaptability to technological change.
Why It Matters
Differences in technical literacy exclude some users because operation is too complex or too hard to understand. Accounting for technical literacy helps design products or services that are easy to pick up, cheap to learn, and tolerant of different experience levels, improving accessibility and user satisfaction.
Related Standards and References

ISO 9241-210: human-centred design (covering user ability and experience)
WCAG 2.1: understandability and operability guidance (consistency, error prevention, help documentation)
Usability principles from human-computer interaction: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, satisfaction
Digital literacy frameworks from institutions such as Peking University
Digital-inclusion guidance in national aging-response policies

Suggested Quantification Methods

Self-report scales: e.g., technology proficiency questionnaires (such as Pew Research Center’s technology-use index)
Performance measures: task completion time, error counts, frequency of help-seeking
Learning curves: first-use success rate, improvement after repeated use
Substitution rates: e.g., the share of users choosing a voice assistant over touch
Data sources: user surveys, usability testing, interviews, behavioral log analysis

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: intuitive onboarding, progressive feature exposure, consistent interaction patterns, clear visual cues, undo and redo
Industrial design: simplified control panels, unambiguous operating indicators, misuse-proof design, ease of maintenance and servicing
Architectural design: clarity of signage systems, usage instructions for elevators and facilities, easily understood emergency evacuation routes
Interior design: affordance cues on furniture and fixtures, simplicity of smart-home interfaces
Graphic design: clear information hierarchy, obvious reading order, universally understandable graphic symbols
Fashion design: easy-to-understand wear instructions, clear indicators on adjustable parts, readable care labels

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Assuming all users have above-average technical proficiency
Treating “intuitive” as the designer’s own intuition rather than something tested with target users
Relying on manuals or training to compensate for complex design
Ignoring wide differences in technical literacy across age, education, and region
Focusing only on the first-use experience while ignoring the memory burden of long-term use

Design Recommendation Keywords
Learnability, consistency, salient feedback, error tolerance, progressive disclosure, contextual help, minimal memory burden, reversible actions

Factor card: Technical Literacy
Version: 0.1

factors/who-f-008-cultural-background.title: Cultural Background
factors/who-f-008-cultural-background.content:
Definition
The culture, language, religion, values, customs, and social norms of the user’s context. These factors shape how the user perceives and accepts a design, what usage habits they form, and their communication preferences.
Why It Matters
Cultural differences mean that the same design produces radically different experiences across groups. Ignoring cultural background can cause misunderstanding, offense, or barriers to use. Considering cultural factors helps design products or services that are more relevant, respectful of differences, and easier for a broad range of users to adopt.
Related Standards and References

ISO 9241-210: human-centred design process (considering the usage context, including culture)
Hofstede’s cultural dimensions theory (power distance, individualism, etc.)
Common language standards: Unicode, BCP 47 language tags
WCAG 2.1: language of parts (lang attribute), comprehensibility guidance
Language requirements in accessibility legislation across jurisdictions (e.g., Canada’s multilingual services)

Suggested Quantification Methods

Language coverage: number of supported languages, share of target users’ native languages covered
Cultural fit: degree of conformity with cultural norms measured through user research (e.g., color symbolism, icon comprehension, meaning of gestures)
Localization quality: translation accuracy, correctness of date/time/currency formats, RTL layout support
Cultural sensitivity audit: scores from expert assessment or focus group feedback
Data sources: ethnographic studies, cross-cultural user testing, language distribution data from market research

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: interface language switching, date and time formats, cultural fit of icons and symbols, avoiding cultural color taboos, RTL layout support (Arabic, Hebrew)
Industrial design: product appearance aligned with cultural aesthetics, multilingual instruction manuals, consideration of religious taboos (e.g., food-contact materials, patterns)
Architectural design: spatial layouts that fit social etiquette (e.g., living-room placement, prayer space orientation), cultural sensitivity in decorative patterns
Interior design: furniture arrangements matching cultural usage habits, material choices that account for climate and cultural preferences
Graphic design: typographic direction, fonts supporting multiple scripts, imagery that avoids stereotypes, color pairings informed by cultural meaning
Fashion design: styles conforming to cultural dress norms (e.g., degree of coverage, attire for specific occasions), cultural appropriateness of patterns and symbols, material choices accounting for climate and cultural custom

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Assuming one “globally universal” design and ignoring local differences
Translating the language without considering cultural meaning (jokes, metaphors, references)
Using stereotypes or incorrect cultural symbols
Ignoring the specific needs of ethnic minorities or migrant groups
Ignoring cultural taboos in the use of color, shape, or gestures

Design Recommendation Keywords
Localization, internationalization (i18n), cultural adaptation, symbol review, language switching, RTL layout, cultural consulting, contextual research

Factor card: Cultural Background
Version: 0.1

factors/who-f-009-neurodiversity.title: Neurodiversity
factors/who-f-009-neurodiversity.content:
Basic Definition
Differences in how users’ brains process information, including neurodevelopmental differences such as the autism spectrum, ADHD, dyslexia, and Tourette syndrome, as well as mental health states such as anxiety, depression, and PTSD.
Why It Matters

Neurodivergent people have different needs in perception, attention, social interaction, language, and learning
Ignoring these differences leads to poor experiences, anxiety, and can even trigger adverse reactions
Being inclusive of neurodiversity improves usability for all users (e.g., clearer instructions reduce cognitive load for everyone)

Quantification Criteria

Attention sustainment: average duration of single-task focus, recovery time after being interrupted
Sensory sensitivity: sensitivity thresholds for light, sound, touch, etc. (measurable by scale)
Information processing speed: reading speed, decision time, working memory capacity
Language processing: reading comprehension difficulty, word/character recognition accuracy

Design Guidelines

Provide sensory regulation options (turn off motion, reduce brightness, lower sound)
Avoid sudden changes (flashing, unexpected sounds)
Provide clear, consistent navigation and feedback
Let users control the pace (pause, replay, skip)
Provide multi-channel information (text, icons, speech as options)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainAdaptive DesignDigital productsFocus mode, reduced animation, simplified interfaces, gentler error messagesWorkspacesNoise-cancelling headphones, individual workstations, flexible working hoursArchitectural spacesQuiet retreat corners, clear signage, controllable lighting, reduced background noiseFashion designTagless clothing, soft fabrics, non-restrictive cuts, predictable dressing and undressing steps
Related Standards

WCAG 2.3: no flashing (seizures)
ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) covers part of the neurodiversity scope
Various national mental health and anti-discrimination regulations


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (increasingly important)

factors/who-f-010-cognitive-traits.title: Cognitive Traits
factors/who-f-010-cognitive-traits.content:
Definition
Users’ psychological functioning traits in perception, attention, memory, language, problem solving, and decision making — individual differences in processing speed, working memory capacity, attention span, executive function, and language comprehension and expression.
Why It Matters
The diversity of cognitive ability directly affects how users understand information, learn to operate a product, make decisions, and complete tasks. Ignoring cognitive differences can lead to information overload, confusion, or task failure — most markedly for older adults, children, and people with learning disabilities or neurodivergence. Considering cognitive traits helps design products or services that are easy to understand, simple to operate, and low in cognitive load.
Subtypes and Specific Dimensions
Processing Speed

Simple/choice reaction time, information extraction speed, reading speed, decision latency

Working Memory and Attention

Digit/alphanumeric span, sustained attention (CPT), task-switching cost, interference-suppression ability

Executive Function

Planning and organization, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, maintenance of goal-directed behavior

Language Comprehension and Expression

Vocabulary breadth, comprehension of syntactic complexity, metaphor/idiom comprehension, cost of switching between languages

Numeracy

Reinforced by the B1 cross-reference pass (INCL-XREF-001, cross-referenced against WCAG COGA requirements)


Quantity representation (estimation/precise calculation), spatial-numerical reasoning (geometry/chart comprehension), financial literacy (interest/compound interest/risk probability)
Related disabilities: developmental dyscalculia, acquired dyscalculia, math anxiety
Design response: avoid tasks requiring mental arithmetic, provide calculators/automatic calculation, replace numeric comparison with visualization, automatic currency/unit conversion

Spatial Cognition

Mental rotation, navigation/route planning, object localization, visuospatial working memory

Neurodiversity-Related Traits

ADHD: attention regulation, impulse control, time perception
Autism spectrum: sensory processing, social cognition, reliance on routine, special interests
Dyslexia: phonological processing, rapid naming, spelling
Motor coordination disorders: motor planning, bimanual coordination

Related Standards and References

WCAG 2.1: understandability principle (e.g., readability of language, predictability, input assistance)
ISO 9241-210: human-centred design (considering user abilities)
Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller et al.)
Common cognitive assessment instruments: e.g., the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE)
Guidance from neurodiversity advocacy organizations (e.g., autism associations, ADHD resources)
Working memory and processing-speed models in educational psychology

Suggested Quantification Methods

Processing speed: reaction-time tests (e.g., simple reaction time, choice reaction time)
Working memory capacity: digit span, alphanumeric span tests
Attention span: continuous performance test (CPT), task-switching cost
Executive function: Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Stroop test
Language comprehension: vocabulary tests, sentence comprehension accuracy
Numeracy: numerical comparison tasks, arithmetic fluency tests, number-line estimation tasks
Subjective load: NASA-TLX, Subjective Workload Assessment Technique (SWAT)
Data sources: standard procedures for psychological experiments, clinical neuropsychological tests, performance metrics from user usability testing

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: chunked information, step-by-step guidance, fewer menu levels, familiar paradigms, undo and redo, clear error messages that include repair suggestions
Industrial design: simple control interfaces, few operating steps, salient feedback, interlock designs that prevent misoperation
Architectural design: clear signage systems, logical floor numbering, intuitive emergency egress routes
Interior design: furniture whose function is apparent at a glance, switch positions that match habits, reachable storage space
Graphic design: clear information hierarchy, natural visual flow, avoiding information overload, symbol-assisted comprehension
Fashion design: simple dressing and undressing steps, clear size labels, easy to follow care instructions (e.g., using graphic symbols)

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Equating “intuitive” with the designer’s own familiarity rather than testing with target users
Over-relying on textual explanations while neglecting the supporting role of graphics or demonstrations
Ignoring the cumulative effect of cognitive fatigue over long-term use
Considering only extreme cognitive impairment (e.g., dementia) while ignoring mild or situational increases in cognitive load (e.g., multitasking, high-pressure environments)
Failing to account for the additional burden of language processing in multilingual or cross-cultural scenarios

Design Recommendation Keywords
Reduced cognitive load, information layering, consistency, predictability, timely feedback, error tolerance, progressive disclosure, familiar patterns, plain language, visual aids

Factor card: Cognitive Traits
Version: 3.1 (B1 reinforcement: numeracy cognition subtype)

factors/who-f-011-language.title: Language
factors/who-f-011-language.content:
Definition
Users’ native language, proficiency in the languages they use, literacy level, and ability to understand specific language varieties (dialects, terminology). Language affects how information is acquired, understood, and expressed.
Why It Matters
Language barriers are a primary obstacle to accessing information and using services. If a design depends only on a particular language, it excludes users who do not speak that language or are not proficient enough in it. Considering language factors supports multilingual support, plain language, and varying literacy levels, improving both information accessibility and service usability.
Subtypes and Specific Dimensions
Language Variation (linguistic level)

Native language and second-language proficiency: CEFR levels, academic/professional language competence
Dialects/regional varieties: lexical differences, grammatical differences, differences in pragmatic rules
Multilingual environments: code-switching, language preference settings, fallback language strategy

Literacy (literacy level)

Literacy level: non-literate, low literacy, functional illiteracy, high literacy
Reading disorders: developmental dyslexia, alexia (acquired reading disorder)
Writing disorders: writing expression disorder, apraxia of writing

Speech-Motor Impairment vs. Language Variation

Reinforced by the B1 cross-reference pass (INCL-XREF-001, cross-referenced against WHO ICF b3 and WCAG speech requirements)

Key distinction:






























DimensionSpeech-Motor Impairment (articulation/phonation)Language Variation (linguistic/cognitive)EssenceDifficulty producing speech at the motor-execution levelDifference or disorder in the language system (vocabulary/grammar/pragmatics)Typical manifestationsUnclear articulation, abnormal speech rate, abnormal voice quality, restricted movement of the articulatory organsLimited vocabulary, grammatical errors, comprehension difficulties, pragmatic inappropriatenessRelated disabilitiesArticulation disorders, apraxia of speech, laryngectomy, vocal cord paralysis, stutteringAphasia, specific language impairment (SLI), difficulty in second-language acquisitionDesign responseAlternative speech input (text/gesture/eye tracking), speech-independent authentication, speech-synthesis outputMultilingual UI, plain readable text, symbol-assisted communication, term base, translation
Design principle: do not conflate the two kinds of needs. Users with speech-motor impairment may have intact language ability and only need an alternative input channel; users with language variation may pronounce clearly but need language-level adaptation.
Related Standards and References

WCAG 2.1: language of parts (lang attribute), comprehensibility guidance (e.g., avoiding overly complex language)
ISO 9241-210: human-centred design (considering users’ language and culture)
The Unicode standard, BCP 47 language tags
National language-rights legislation (e.g., Canada’s Official Languages Act)
Plain Language principles

Suggested Quantification Methods

Language coverage: number of supported languages, share of target users’ native languages covered
Readability assessment: e.g., Flesch-Kincaid grade level, Gunning fog index, SMOG index
Translation quality: back-translation accuracy, terminology consistency scores
Language proficiency assessment: user self-assessment or standardized tests (e.g., CEFR)
Data sources: census language distribution, immigration authorities’ language-service demand, user surveys

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: UI language switching, content translation, multilingual speech output, locale-adapted error messages
Industrial design: multilingual instruction manuals, warning labels that use graphic symbols to reduce language dependence
Architectural design: multilingual signage systems, emergency egress graphic symbols, language options on service signage
Interior design: multilingual furniture instruction manuals, language support for smart-home apps
Graphic design: multilingual print versions, fonts supporting multilingual character sets, symbol-first information hierarchy
Fashion design: multilingual care labels, international-standard size charts, pictorial care instructions

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Assuming that English or one dominant language can cover all users
Providing language switching without accounting for cultural differences between languages (e.g., date formats, honorifics)
Ignoring low-literacy users or users with reading disorders while over-relying on text
Using machine translation without human review, causing misunderstanding or discourtesy
Failing to consider differences in cultural meaning when using icons or colors
Conflating speech-motor impairment with language variation: demanding that users with articulation disorders “speak the standard language,” or offering non-native users speech recognition instead of translation

Design Recommendation Keywords
Multilingual support, plain language, graphic symbols, language switching, culturally aware translation, RTL layout, speech output, term base

Factor card: Language
Version: 3.1 (B1 reinforcement: distinguishing speech-motor impairment from language variation)

factors/who-f-012-literacy.title: Literacy
factors/who-f-012-literacy.content:
Definition
Users’ ability to recognize, understand, use, and create written information, including basic letter recognition, word decoding, sentence comprehension, paragraph reading, and written expression. Literacy level affects how users acquire information and interact through text.
Why It Matters
Differences in literacy directly determine whether users can understand interface text, instruction text, error messages, and content information. Low-literacy users may rely on graphics, icons, or speech interaction. Considering literacy helps design products or services that present information in varied forms, in clear layers, and without depending on a high level of literacy.
Related Standards and References

WCAG 2.1: understandability principle (e.g., readability of language, avoiding overly complex language)
UNESCO literacy-rate standards
Adult education frameworks
Plain Language principles
Literacy assessment standards from national education departments

Suggested Quantification Methods

Literacy assessment: e.g., the National Assessment of Adult Literacy (NAAL), the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC)
Text difficulty assessment: e.g., Flesch-Kincaid grade level, Gunning fog index, SMOG index
Comprehension testing: measuring the proportion of users who correctly understand presented information
Preference measurement: users’ preference for graphic vs. textual information
Data sources: education surveys, censuses, comprehension performance in user testing

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: icon-assisted comprehension, speech read-aloud options, chunked information, tiered headings, avoiding long paragraphs of text
Industrial design: manual instructions using graphic symbols, warning labels using color coding and graphics, illustrated assembly steps
Architectural design: signage systems using universally understood graphics, room numbers paired with symbols, pictorial emergency evacuation guidance
Interior design: illustrated furniture assembly instructions, easy step-by-step diagrams in instruction manuals
Graphic design: clear information hierarchy, symbols and graphics assisting comprehension, color coding to support information classification
Fashion design: international symbols on size labels, graphic symbols for care instructions (e.g., washing, drying)

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Assuming all users have literacy at or above secondary-school level
Over-relying on text without providing multiple forms of information presentation
Considering only first-language literacy while ignoring differences in second languages or dialects
Equating “non-literate” with “unable to understand any information,” ignoring alternative graphic and speech channels
Failing to account for regional literacy differences in global products, making information unreachable

Design Recommendation Keywords
Plain language, graphic support, speech output, information layering, symbol use, color coding, jargon-free terminology, multimodal presentation

Factor card: Literacy
Version: 0.1

factors/who-f-013-body-size-ergonomics.title: Body Size & Ergonomics
factors/who-f-013-body-size-ergonomics.content:
Basic Definition
Users’ body dimensions (height, arm length, finger span, etc.) and ergonomic characteristics such as joint range of motion, strength, and endurance.
Why It Matters

When equipment or space does not match the user’s body dimensions, it easily causes fatigue, operational difficulty, or injury
Users of extreme height or particular body types may be entirely unable to use a product (e.g., overly tall users hitting door frames)
Accounting for the diversity of human dimensions improves universal comfort

Quantification Criteria

Percentile reference: anthropometric data at the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles
Adjustment range: the adjustable range and method of seat height, desk height, and screen tilt
Operating force: the pressing force required by buttons, the rotational torque of handles
Reach envelope: whether operating parts fall within the user’s reach

Design Guidelines

Provide adjustable physical structures (desk and chair, mounts, handles)
Key operating positions should cover the reach envelope of the majority of the population
Avoid operations requiring great force or fine control (unless necessary and with an alternative provided)
Consider special body types such as pregnancy, children, and wheelchair users

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainKey ConsiderationsDigital productsDevice dimensions and grip feel, touch target size (minimum 44×44pt)Industrial designTool handle diameter, operating force, control panel layoutArchitectural designDoor frame height, countertop height, stair riser dimensions, handrail positionFashion designSize-range coverage, adjustable parts (waist, leg length)
Related Standards

ISO 7250: basic human body measurements
ANSI/HFES 100: human factors engineering data
WCAG 2.5.5: Target Size (touch)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (essential to all physical-interaction design)

factors/who-f-014-privacy-security-conce.title: Privacy & Security Concerns
factors/who-f-014-privacy-security-conce.content:
Definition
The degree of users’ concern and worry, when using a product or service, that personal information may be leaked, tracked, or misused, and that physical safety may be threatened — including feelings about data privacy, anonymity, protection from harassment, and physical safety.
Why It Matters
Privacy and security concerns directly determine whether users are willing to adopt, trust, and continue using a product or service. Even a functionally powerful product can lead to abandonment or a switch to a competitor if users feel unsafe or that their privacy is violated. Considering privacy and security helps design products or services that are trustworthy, respect user autonomy, and reduce worry.
Related Standards and References

Data privacy regulations such as GDPR, CCPA, and PIPL
ISO/IEC 27001: information security management
Privacy by Design principles
Security-usability research (e.g., phishing-attack prevention)
National cybersecurity laws

Suggested Quantification Methods

Subjective concern scores: measuring users’ level of privacy and security concern using scales (e.g., privacy concern scales)
Behavioral indicators: whether users provide only the minimum necessary information, use anonymous mode, and the rate of consent withdrawal
Technical implementation: degree of data encryption, adherence to the principle of least privilege, whether third-party privacy certification is obtained
Incident records: privacy complaints, data-breach incidents, time to fix security vulnerabilities
Data sources: user surveys, behavioral logs, security audit reports, transparency reports

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: data minimization collection, explicit privacy policies, opt-out of tracking, end-to-end encryption, anonymous login options
Industrial design: whether the product includes anti-tamper design, whether usage data is collected and how users are told about it
Architectural design: explicit signage of surveillance cameras and usage policies, transparency of access-control systems
Interior design: data-usage explanations for smart-home devices, wake-word privacy modes for voice assistants
Graphic design: whether advertising avoids making users feel tracked (e.g., overly targeted ads)
Fashion design: whether the collection and transmission methods of smart-garment data are transparent and disableable by users

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Assuming that users will sacrifice privacy as long as the product works well
Considering privacy only when legally required rather than proactively building trust
Privacy policies that are too long and full of legal jargon for users to understand
Failing to provide enough control options when personalization features are needed
Equating anonymity with loss of function instead of designing a controllable degree of sharing

Design Recommendation Keywords
Data minimization, transparency, user control, anonymous options, security by design, trust building, privacy dashboard, consent management, minimum-necessary principle

Factor card: Privacy & Security Concerns
