factors/who-f-015-gender-expression.title: Gender & Gender Expression
factors/who-f-015-gender-expression.content:
Definition
Differences in the gender dimension as users are identified, addressed, and presented within a system, product, or space, including:

Sex: the biological attributes at birth, which affect dimensions and physiological needs (e.g., sanitary facilities)
Gender identity: the gender a person self-identifies with, which may differ from the sex assigned at birth (transgender, non-binary, etc.)
Gender expression: outwardly displayed gender presentation (clothing, hairstyle, mannerisms), which may not align with one’s identity
Gender-neutral needs: users who do not identify with binary gender categories

Distinction from other factors: WHO-F-002 (demographics) carries only statistical attributes (age/regional distribution); this factor carries the concrete differences of gender at the interaction and presentation levels.
Why It Matters

Mandatory binary gender fields in forms (single-choice male/female) directly exclude non-binary users
Honorific systems (Mr./Ms.) assume that gender can be inferred from a name or appearance
The binary division of restrooms, fitting rooms, and size systems creates spatial exclusion
Historical data (e.g., medical insurance, ticketing) gender records may not match current identity

Design Response (both: alternatives + choice space)
Capability/constraint components → provide alternatives

Gender fields should offer a “prefer not to say / X / custom” option (a compliance requirement in many jurisdictions)
Honorific fields should be optional, or provide gender-neutral honorifics

Preference components → provide choice space

Gender visibility in profiles should be configurable (public / private only / visible to specific people)
Respect users’ chosen pronouns and use them consistently in the UI

Cross-Domain Mapping






























DomainExclusion ExampleInclusion ExampleDigital productsMandatory binary gender registration fieldOptional gender field + custom input + pronoun fieldIndustrial designGrips designed for the “male hand”Adjustable grips; neutral size rangesArchitectural designRestrooms split male/female onlyAt least one all-gender/family restroom (many building codes already require this)Fashion designSize charts split by binary genderA size system based on body measurements (chest/waist circumference) rather than gender
Measurement Dimensions

Completeness of gender-field options in forms (whether non-binary/prefer-not-to-say options exist)
Configurability of honorifics/pronouns
Availability of gender-neutral options in physical facilities

Related Standards and References

UD7 supplementary principles P8 (Community) and P10 (Gender)
WHO ICF personal factors
Compliance requirements in some jurisdictions (e.g., Argentina’s Gender Identity Law, ESG reporting requirements at some companies) → pending WP-C linkage to specific clauses

B1 Cross-Reference Note
This factor was added as new by the INCL-XREF-001 GAP-1 determination: only the UD7 supplementary principles implicitly mention gender among the 5 baseline frameworks, and none of them structured it as a factor.

factors/why-f-001-cost-constraint.title: Cost Constraint
factors/why-f-001-cost-constraint.content:
Definition
The financial limits involved in designing, producing, distributing, and maintaining a product or service, including material costs, manufacturing expenses, R&D investment, regulatory compliance costs, and the target selling price or budget ceiling.
Why It Matters
Cost is a core factor in commercial viability. Ignoring cost constraints can leave a design technically feasible but economically unsustainable, so it never reaches the market or its target users. Balancing inclusive needs against cost control is key to achieving broad adoption.
Related Standards and References

ISO 9001: quality management systems (cost-effectiveness considerations)
Life-cycle cost analysis (LCCA) in government procurement across jurisdictions
Design for Cost (DFC) methodology
Disability employment and accessibility tax-credit policies (e.g., the Disabled Access Credit in the US)
Social return on investment (SROI) analysis frameworks

Suggested Quantification Methods

Unit cost: material cost, labor cost, manufacturing overhead
Development cost: R&D expenses, testing and certification costs
Compliance cost: the additional investment required to meet a specific standard
Economies-of-scale effect: the drop in unit cost as output increases
Willingness-to-pay (WTP) surveys
Data sources: cost-estimation software, supplier quotes, historical project data, industry benchmarks

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: feature development priorities, third-party service fees, licensing costs, maintenance and update costs
Industrial design: material choice (e.g., plastic vs. metal), manufacturing-process complexity, degree of part standardization
Architectural design: accessibility retrofit costs, elevator installation, cost of dedicated sanitary fixtures
Interior design: prices of aging-friendly furniture, cost of anti-slip flooring materials
Graphic design: multilingual printing costs, cost of special inks or materials
Fashion design: fabric cost for adaptive clothing, cost of bespoke design, feasibility of mass production

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Assuming that inclusive design necessarily increases cost, ignoring the scale benefits and spillover returns that universal design brings
Looking only at upfront investment while ignoring savings in long-term maintenance, support, and avoided retrofit cost
Failing to account for the affordability and market size of different user groups
Over-optimizing cost in the early concept stage, making it hard to add necessary accessibility features later

Design Recommendation Keywords
Cost-benefit analysis, universal design, platformization, modularization, life-cycle cost, economies of scale, prioritization matrix, optional features

Factor card: Cost Constraint
Version: 0.1

factors/why-f-002-market-positioning.title: Market Positioning
factors/why-f-002-market-positioning.content:
Definition
The competitive position of a product or service in its target market — including target customer segments, value proposition, differentiation advantages, pricing strategy, and brand image — which determines its appeal and competitiveness in a given segment.
Why It Matters
Market positioning directly affects a product’s commercial success and sustainability. Ignoring market positioning can leave an inclusive design usable but unable to attract enough users or generate profit, making it hard to scale. Considering market positioning helps combine inclusive features with target users’ needs, willingness to pay, and brand expectations, balancing social and commercial value.
Related Standards and References

Porter’s Five Forces model
STP marketing theory (segmentation, targeting, positioning)
Business Model Canvas (value propositions, customer relationships, revenue streams)
Kano model (basic needs, performance needs, delight needs)
Social enterprise and B Corp assessment criteria
Social value weighting in government procurement across jurisdictions

Suggested Quantification Methods

Target market size: TAM (total addressable market), SAM (serviceable available market), SOM (serviceable obtainable market)
Users’ willingness to pay a premium for inclusive features (WTP surveys)
Brand perception surveys: awareness and favorability within the target group
Differentiation index: advantage scores over competitors on inclusive dimensions
Revenue forecasting: financial models based on pricing strategy and market penetration rate
Data sources: market research reports, competitor analysis, user interviews, industry benchmarks

Manifestations Across Domains

Digital products: inclusive features as paid entry points in freemium models, enterprise-level accessibility compliance as a selling point, audience coverage for advertising-supported apps
Industrial design: ergonomic premium in the high-end market, cost-benefit balance in the mass market, compliance with accessibility standards in government procurement
Architectural design: accessibility upscale finishes in luxury residences, statutory minimums for public buildings, cost-sharing for aging-friendly retrofits in the rental market
Interior design: anthropometric fit in high-end bespoke furniture, conformance with universal design standards in the wholesale market
Graphic design: readability and recognizability within brand VI systems, precise reach of target groups in public-interest advertising
Fashion design: basic adaptability in mass fast fashion, individualized accessibility needs in high-end bespoke, balance between functionality and professional image for workwear

Common Misconceptions and Blind Spots

Seeing inclusion as belonging only to charity or compliance, ignoring its potential as an innovation and differentiation advantage
Catering only to the most demanding standards while ignoring most users’ actual acceptance and willingness to pay
Focusing excessively on technical implementation in the early concept stage while ignoring market validation
Failing to account for positioning differences across channels (online vs. offline, B2B vs. B2C)
Treating inclusion as an add-on feature rather than part of the core value proposition

Design Recommendation Keywords
Value proposition fit, willingness to pay for accessibility, brand inclusivity, differentiating features, target-group personas, universal pricing models, social value quantification, go-to-market strategy

Factor card: Market Positioning
Version: 0.1

factors/why-f-003-business-model.title: Business Model
factors/why-f-003-business-model.content:
Basic Definition
How a product monetizes and captures value — one-time purchase, subscription, freemium, licensing, platform take rate, advertising monetization, and so on — along with the design constraints these create.
Why It Matters

The business model directly determines trade-offs in product functionality, the scope of user data collection, and the boundaries of experience design
Under different models users’ willingness to pay and expectations differ, which affects the priority of inclusive needs
A balance must be struck between profit goals and user value

Quantification Criteria

Revenue-source distribution: the share of each source (subscription, advertising, transaction take rate, etc.)
User conversion funnel: trial → paid conversion rate
ARPU/LTV: average revenue per user and lifetime value
Price sensitivity: users’ response to price changes (elasticity)

Design Guidelines

Clearly distinguish free from paid functionality in the design
Avoid monetization design that overly interferes with the core experience (e.g., ads that obstruct)
Provide flexible payment options (monthly/yearly, student discounts)
Consider alternative value-acquisition paths for users with limited ability to pay (time for money, tasks for benefits)

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainManifestationSaaS softwareSubscription tiers, collaboration seat limits, advanced feature tiersHardware productsAccessory profits, consumable repurchase, software-service bundlingPlatform economiesTake rate, subsidy strategy, member privilegesPublic servicesFree basics, value-added services, usage-based billing
Related Standards

Industry best practices (e.g., freemium design patterns)
Research on pricing ethics and fairness


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (a core business decision)

factors/why-f-004-sustainability-goals.title: Sustainability & Environmental Goals
factors/why-f-004-sustainability-goals.content:
Basic Definition
A product’s or service’s environmental impact across its entire life cycle — including energy consumption, carbon emissions, waste generation, and material recyclability — along with the environmental goals the organization sets.
Why It Matters

Environmental regulation is tightening, and carbon emissions are becoming a trade barrier
Consumers and investors increasingly focus on ESG performance
Green design can lower long-term operating costs (e.g., energy savings)
It embodies corporate social responsibility and raises brand value

Quantification Criteria

Carbon footprint: carbon emissions across the production, transport, use, and disposal stages
Energy efficiency: energy consumption per unit of functionality (e.g., per GB of data transfer)
Waste rate: the proportion of recyclable vs. non-recyclable parts
Material sourcing: share of renewable/recycled materials, conflict-minerals screening

Design Guidelines

Choose low-carbon materials and processes
Provide a “green mode” (energy saving, low power, reduced non-essential output)
Optimize logistics and packaging (reduce volume and weight, use reusable packaging)
Extend product life (repairable, upgradable, modular)
Provide end-of-life recycling channels for products

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainSustainable Design PointsDigital servicesGreen energy for data centers, code efficiency, reduced data transfer volumesHardware devicesLow-power chips, removable batteries, modular design, easily recyclable materialsApparel and textilesOrganic cotton, recycled fibers, rental models, secondhand circulationArchitectural spacesPassive energy efficiency, solar utilization, rainwater harvesting, green building materials
Related Standards

ISO 14001: environmental management systems
GHG Protocol: greenhouse gas accounting
Eco-labels such as the EU Ecolabel and Energy Star


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (brand- and regulation-driven)

factors/why-f-005-stakeholder-impact.title: Stakeholder Impact
factors/why-f-005-stakeholder-impact.content:
Basic Definition
The needs, expectations, and power dynamics of the various groups a product or service affects or is affected by (users, customers, partners, regulators, internal teams, communities, and so on).
Why It Matters

Design decisions must satisfy not only end users but also customers, channel partners, compliance stakeholders, and others
Ignoring key stakeholders can lead to market resistance, legal risk, or resource damage
Balancing competing interests is a common challenge in complex design tasks

Quantification Criteria

Stakeholder map: positioning on two dimensions — power and level of interest
Need-conflict degree: the level of misalignment between different groups’ needs (high/medium/low)
Impact score: the magnitude of the positive or negative impact of a design change on each group
Support level: the strength of each group’s support for or opposition to a design proposal

Design Guidelines

Identify core users vs. paying customers (which may differ)
Design customized views or features for different roles (e.g., administrators vs. ordinary members)
Establish feedback mechanisms that let all parties participate
Make the basis for decisions transparent, explaining trade-offs

Cross-Domain Manifestations

























DomainExamples of Competing DemandsEnterprise softwareManagement needs reports, employees need convenience, IT needs securitySocial platformsUsers need freedom of expression, regulators need compliance, advertisers need exposureHealthcare systemsPatients need privacy, clinicians need efficiency, hospitals need cost controlEducational productsStudents need engagement, teachers need instructional management, schools need procurement compliance
Related Standards

Stakeholder theory (Freeman)
Stakeholder management in project management (PMBOK)


Factor weight assessment: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (essential for B2B/complex systems)
